naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to an interview with Sara Lindqvist, who started a natural skincare company at her kitchen table. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Sara, your company now sells skincare products in fourteen countries. But it all started in a kitchen, didn't it?

Sara: It did – a very small kitchen in a student flat in Edinburgh. I was studying chemistry, and I had terrible problems with my skin. Every cream I bought from the chemist's made it worse. So one evening I thought, I'm a chemistry student, why don't I make my own?

Interviewer: What did you use?

Sara: Very simple things at first: oats, honey, olive oil and a little beeswax that I bought from a farmer at the weekend market. My flatmates complained that the whole flat smelled like breakfast. But after three weeks my skin was better than it had been for years.

Interviewer: When did you realise it could become a business?

Sara: Honestly, I didn't plan it. I gave a few jars to friends as birthday presents, and then their friends started asking for them. By the end of my second year, I was selling about fifty jars a month, mostly through social media. I kept the money in a biscuit tin under my bed.

Interviewer: That's a long way from fourteen countries.

Sara: It is. The real turning point came when I finished university. I had a job offer from a big pharmaceutical company, with a good salary, and my parents were very keen for me to take it. Instead, I borrowed four thousand pounds from my grandmother and rented a tiny unit on an industrial estate. My parents thought I'd gone mad.

Interviewer: Were they right?

Sara: For the first year, it certainly looked like it. I made every mistake possible. Once I ordered two thousand glass jars and they arrived with the wrong lids. Another time a whole batch of cream went off because the unit got too hot in summer. I worked seven days a week and paid myself almost nothing. There were nights when I cried in the car park.

Interviewer: What kept you going?

Sara: The customers, really. People wrote to me – real letters, sometimes – saying that my cream had helped their child's eczema or that they finally felt comfortable in their own skin. You can't give up when you read something like that.

Interviewer: And then came the big break.

Sara: Yes. A well-known beauty journalist bought one of our creams in a little shop in the Highlands and wrote about it in a national newspaper. The next morning our website crashed. We received more orders in one weekend than in the whole previous year. I had to ask my mum, my aunt and two neighbours to help me pack boxes.

Interviewer: So your parents changed their minds?

Sara: My mum now works for the company three days a week! She's in charge of customer letters, because she says I'm too slow at answering them.

Interviewer: What's important to you now that the company is bigger?

Sara: That we don't forget where we started. We still use mostly local ingredients, all our packaging can be recycled, and we never test on animals. And every new product is still tested first in a kitchen – my own.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to young people who want to start a business?

Sara: Start small and start now. Don't wait until you have a perfect plan, because you never will. And keep your day costs low – I didn't buy a new car or a fancy office for six years.

Interviewer: Sara, thank you very much.

Sara: Thank you.

A young entrepreneur

As you listen to the recording, decide whether the following statements are true (T) or false (F).

  1. 0.Sara was studying chemistry when she made her first cream. (T)
  2. 1.Sara bought her first ingredients at a market. T / F
  3. 2.Sara's flatmates liked the smell of her products. T / F
  4. 3.Sara started selling her creams because she had a business plan. T / F
  5. 4.Sara's parents wanted her to accept a job offer. T / F
  6. 5.Sara's grandmother lent her money to start the business. T / F
  7. 6.In the first year, a batch of cream was spoiled by the heat. T / F
  8. 7.A journalist discovered Sara's cream in a shop in Edinburgh. T / F
  9. 8.Sara's mother now answers letters from customers. T / F
  10. 9.Sara advises young people to wait until they have a perfect plan. T / F

1. T
2. F
3. F
4. T
5. T
6. T
7. F
8. T
9. F
naloge.razlaga:
Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take
  • Kaj zahteva naloga: med poslušanjem odločiti, ali je trditev pravilna (T) ali napačna (F).
  • Postopek: pred poslušanjem preberi trditve in podčrtaj ključne besede (števila, imena, nikalnice, always/never). Trditve si sledijo v vrstnem redu posnetka.
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: razlaga navede, kaj je govorec rekel. Trditev je F, če se v eni podrobnosti razlikuje od posnetka (drug čas, druga oseba, drug razlog).

Spodaj je pri vsaki postavki rešitev in razlaga, ki pokaže, kje v besedilu ali posnetku je odgovor in katero pravilo velja.

»a little beeswax that I bought from a farmer at the weekend market«.

»My flatmates complained that the whole flat smelled like breakfast.«
3. F
»Honestly, I didn't plan it.« – začelo se je z darili prijateljem.
4. T
»my parents were very keen for me to take it«.

»I borrowed four thousand pounds from my grandmother«.
6. T
»a whole batch of cream went off because the unit got too hot in summer«.

Kremo je kupila v trgovinici v škotskem višavju (the Highlands).

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to a conversation with Tom Haddon and Elena Ruiz, who run a repair café in Bristol. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Presenter: In today's programme, we're talking about repair cafés – places where people bring broken things and volunteers help them fix them for free. With me are Tom Haddon and Elena Ruiz, who run one in Bristol. Tom, what exactly happens at a repair café?

Tom: Once a month, on the first Saturday, we take over a church hall for four hours. People arrive with whatever is broken – toasters, lamps, bicycles, jumpers with holes, even children's toys – and they sit down with one of our volunteers. The important thing is that we don't just repair things for people. They sit next to the volunteer and learn how to do it themselves.

Presenter: Elena, how did you get involved?

Elena: By accident, really. My grandmother's sewing machine stopped working, and every shop I went to told me it was too old to repair and that I should buy a new one. A friend told me about the repair café, so I went along. A retired engineer called Frank opened it up, found a tiny broken spring and fixed it in twenty minutes. I was so impressed that I signed up as a volunteer the same day.

Presenter: And now you run the café together.

Elena: Yes, for the last three years. Tom does the organising and I'm in charge of the textiles table – clothes, curtains, bags, that kind of thing.

Presenter: Tom, who are your volunteers?

Tom: All kinds of people. Many of them are retired – electricians, engineers, tailors – who have a lifetime of skills and want to use them. But we also have students, and one of our best bicycle mechanics is only fifteen. What they share is that they hate throwing things away.

Presenter: What are the most common repairs?

Tom: Electrical items, definitely. Vacuum cleaners, hair dryers, coffee machines. Very often the problem is something simple, like a loose wire or a blown fuse. Last year we kept a record and found that we managed to repair about two thirds of everything people brought in.

Presenter: And the other third?

Tom: Sometimes we can't get the spare part, or the product has been designed so that you can't open it without breaking it. That's one of our biggest frustrations. Some manufacturers glue their products together so that you can't change a battery, for example.

Elena: Which is why we also campaign for what's called the "right to repair" – laws that make companies sell spare parts and provide repair manuals. Things are starting to change, but slowly.

Presenter: Is it really about the environment, or is it about saving money?

Elena: Both, but I'd say it's also about community. People come for a repair and stay for the tea and cake. We have customers who come every month even when they've got nothing broken, just to chat. For some older people who live alone, it's the only social event in their month.

Tom: And there's something very satisfying about it. People arrive looking worried, holding a broken lamp that belonged to their mother, and they leave smiling. You can't buy that feeling in a shop.

Presenter: What would you say to someone who wants to start a repair café in their town?

Tom: Find a free space, a few people with skills, and a lot of tea. You don't need much money. And make sure you have insurance – that's the boring but important part.

Elena: And don't be afraid of not knowing everything. Half the time we learn together with the customer. I couldn't fix anything when I started.

Presenter: Tom, Elena, thank you very much.

Repair cafés

As you listen to the recording, answer in note form in the spaces below.

    In a church hall.
  2. 1.How often does the repair café take place?

  8. 7.What proportion of items did they manage to repair last year?
  9. 8.What does the 'right to repair' campaign want companies to provide?
  10. 9.According to Tom, what is boring but important when starting a repair café?

deli.A: A) PISNI SESTAVEK (V ENI OD STALNIH SPOROČANJSKIH OBLIK)

naloge.besedilo:
Report

You came first in an international online science competition for secondary school students. Your prize was a week at the Young Scientists' Summer Camp in Cambridge, England. After returning home, you have been asked to write a report of 120–150 words for the organisers of the competition, in which you

  • explain which activity at the camp was the most useful for you and why,
  • describe the social programme,
  • give some feedback on the accommodation and food.
To: Competition Organisers
From: Luka Novak
Subject: Young Scientists' Summer Camp
naloge.rezultat: Formalno poročilo z glavo, uvodom z namenom, odstavki s podnaslovi (najbolj koristna dejavnost z utemeljitvijo, družabni program, nastanitev in hrana s povratno informacijo) in sklepom; 120–150 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Report (120–150 words), formal style
  2. explain which activity at the camp was the most useful for you and why
  3. describe the social programme
  4. give some feedback on the accommodation and food
Kako napišeš poročilo (report)
Poročilo (report): zgradba
  • Glava: To: (komu) / From: (od koga) / Subject: (zadeva) / Date: (po želji). Nagovora »Dear …« ni.
  • Naslov ali kratek uvod z namenom: The aim/purpose of this report is to … / This report summarises …
  • Odstavki s podnaslovi: vsaka iztočnica dobi svoj odstavek z jasnim podnaslovom (Host family, School, Recommendations).
  • Sklep ali priporočila: Overall, … / I would recommend … / It would be a good idea to …
Slog poročila
  • Formalen, stvaren, jedrnat: dejstva, številke, ocene z utemeljitvijo.
  • Pogosti so trpnik in neosebni izrazi: The event was attended by … / It was felt that … / Most participants agreed that …
  • Ocena naj bo uravnotežena: pohvala in kritika (The timetable was well organised; however, …).
  • Ni skrajšanih oblik, ni čustvenih vzklikov. Prva oseba (I, we) je dovoljena, a besedilo naj ne zveni kot dnevnik.
Uporabne zveze
  • The aim of this report is to … · This report is based on …
  • The most successful part was … because … · One drawback was …
  • I would strongly recommend … · In conclusion, … · To sum up, …
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Zgradba poročila
To: Competition Organisers / From: Luka Novak / Subject: Young Scientists' Summer Camp
Glava in naslov; ni nagovora »Dear …«.
Introduction – The purpose of this report is to describe my week at the camp.
Uvod z namenom.
The most useful activity
The laboratory workshop on DNA, where we carried out our own experiments with real equipment.
Iztočnica 1: dejavnost + razlog (because …).
Social programme
Punting on the river, a quiz night, a trip to London.
Iztočnica 2: konkretne dejavnosti.
Accommodation and food
Comfortable single rooms in a college; good breakfasts but few vegetarian options at dinner.
Iztočnica 3: povratna informacija s pohvalo in predlogom.
Conclusion – Overall, the camp was an excellent prize, and I would recommend it.
Kratek sklep.
Preštej besede (120–150).
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
To: Competition Organisers
From: Luka Novak
Subject: Young Scientists' Summer Camp

Introduction

The purpose of this report is to describe my week at the Young Scientists' Summer Camp in Cambridge.

The most useful activity

The most useful activity was the laboratory workshop on DNA. We carried out our own experiments with real equipment, which I had never used at school. It helped me decide that I want to study biology.

Social programme

The social programme was excellent. We went punting on the river, took part in a quiz night and spent a whole day in London.

Accommodation and food

We stayed in comfortable single rooms in one of the colleges. Breakfast was very good, but there were few vegetarian options at dinner, which should be improved.

Conclusion

Overall, the camp was a wonderful prize, and I would highly recommend it to future winners.

Število besed: 143 (zahtevanih 120–150). Zgled je eden od mogočih odgovorov; tvoje besedilo je lahko drugačno, a mora izpolniti vse zahteve iz navodila.

naloge.besedilo:
Choose ONE essay title.

  1. Working together can solve almost any problem.
  2. Social media companies should be responsible for what their users post.

Underline the essay title you have chosen. How far do you agree or disagree with the statement? Support your opinion in 220–250 words.
naloge.rezultat: Argumentativni esej z jasnim stališčem, argumenti s primeri, protiargumentom in sklepom; 220–250 besed, en izbrani naslov.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Choose ONE title and underline it.
  2. State clearly how far you agree or disagree.
  3. Support your opinion with arguments and examples.
  4. Write 220–250 words.
Kako napišeš argumentativni esej
Argumentativni esej: zgradba
  • Uvod (2–3 povedi): uvedi temo s splošno mislijo, trditev iz naslova povej s svojimi besedami in jasno zavzemi stališče (I largely agree that … / I am not convinced that …).
  • Jedro (2–3 odstavki): vsak odstavek ima en argument. Zgradba odstavka: temeljna poved (argument) → razlaga (zakaj drži) → konkreten primer (izkušnja, podatek, primer iz Slovenije).
  • Protiargument: v enem odstavku predstavi nasprotno mnenje in ga ovrzi (Critics argue that … However, …). To pokaže zrelost razmišljanja.
  • Sklep (2–3 povedi): povzemi stališče in odgovori na vprašanje »How far do you agree?«. Brez novih argumentov.
Kako dobiš točke za vsebino
  • Odgovori na naslov, ki si ga izbral, in ga podčrtaj. Ne piši o drugem naslovu.
  • Stališče naj bo jasno in dosledno od uvoda do sklepa. »Deloma se strinjam« je dovoljeno, če pojasniš, v čem da in v čem ne.
  • Primeri morajo biti konkretni: »My cousin spent a year in Ghana …« je boljše kot »Many people do it«.
Uporabne zveze
  • Mnenje: In my opinion, … · I firmly believe that … · It seems to me that …
  • Dodajanje: Furthermore, … · What is more, … · In addition, …
  • Nasprotje: However, … · On the other hand, … · Although …, … · Critics argue that …
  • Primer: For example, … · For instance, … · A good example of this is …
  • Sklep: All things considered, … · To sum up, … · In conclusion, …
Pogoste napake
  • Uvod, ki dobesedno prepiše naslov.
  • Argument brez primera ali primer brez povezave z argumentom.
  • Neformalen slog: you know, a lot of, kids, skrajšane oblike.
  • Prekratko jedro in predolg uvod.
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Načrt (velja za oba naslova)
Uvod: preoblikuj trditev in povej stališče (I largely agree that cooperation can solve most problems, although …).
Teza v uvodu.
Jedro 1: argument + primer (neighbours helping each other after floods; volunteers).
Konkretni primeri.
Jedro 2: argument + primer (scientists from many countries developing vaccines together).
Povezovalci.
Jedro 3: protiargument (some problems need individual courage or a strong leader … However …).
Uravnoteženost.
Sklep: povzemi stališče.
Brez novih argumentov.
Ideje za 2. naslov
For: hate speech and fake news spread quickly; companies earn money from users. Against: freedom of speech, millions of posts, users are responsible for their own words.
Izberi en naslov in ga podčrtaj.
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
Working together can solve almost any problem.

When a flood destroyed several villages in my region a few years ago, hundreds of volunteers arrived the next morning with shovels, food and dry clothes. Within a week, the streets were clean again. Experiences like this convince me that working together can solve almost any problem, although cooperation alone is not always enough.

Firstly, people can achieve far more as a group than alone. One person cannot clean a whole village, but a hundred people can do it in days. At school, too, a team project usually benefits from the different skills of each member.

Secondly, the greatest problems of our time are global. During the pandemic, scientists from many countries shared their data, which helped them develop vaccines in record time. Climate change, too, can only be solved if all countries work together, because pollution does not stop at borders.

On the other hand, cooperation is not always easy. Groups can waste time arguing, and sometimes nobody wants to take responsibility. Sometimes the courage of one person matters more than a committee. However, even the bravest individuals usually depend on the support of others.

In conclusion, I strongly believe that working together is the best way to deal with most problems, from local disasters to global crises. If we learn to listen to each other and share our strengths, there are very few challenges we cannot overcome.

Število besed: 236 (zahtevanih 220–250). Zgled je eden od mogočih odgovorov; tvoje besedilo je lahko drugačno, a mora izpolniti vse zahteve iz navodila.

The Bookshop at the End of the Road

The road to Fjellvik ends where the fjord begins. Beyond the last house there is nothing but water, mountains and, for much of the winter, darkness. It is not the obvious place to open a bookshop. Yet for the past eighteen years, Ingrid Dahl has sold books here, in a red wooden boathouse that once belonged to her grandfather.

Ingrid grew up in the village but left at nineteen to study literature in Oslo. She spent the next fifteen years working for a large publishing company, editing crime novels and travelling to book fairs around the world. "It was exciting," she says, "but I realised that I spent all day talking about books and never had time to read them."

When her grandfather died, he left her the boathouse. Her colleagues expected her to sell it. Instead, she resigned from her job, moved back to Fjellvik and spent a whole summer turning the building into a shop. She built the shelves herself from old fishing boats, and the counter is made from the door of the village's former school.

At first, the locals were doubtful. The village has only about three hundred inhabitants, and the nearest town is two hours away by car. "People told me I would be bankrupt within a year," Ingrid laughs. In the first winter, she sometimes went a whole week without a single customer.

What saved the shop was an unexpected idea. Ingrid began to offer "blind dates with books": novels wrapped in brown paper, with only a few words on the cover to describe them – "a cold country, a lost brother, an ending you will not forget". Customers had to choose without knowing the title or the author. A travel blogger wrote about it, and that summer tourists began to arrive on purpose to buy a mystery book.

Today, the shop receives visitors from all over the world, especially in summer, when the sun hardly sets. Many of them come by boat. Ingrid has added a small reading room with a stove and a view of the fjord, where visitors can sit as long as they like. There is no wifi. "That's not an accident," she says.

In winter, the shop becomes a meeting place for the village. Every Thursday evening there is a reading circle, and children from the local school come once a month to choose books paid for by a fund that Ingrid set up with money from the summer tourists. "In the dark months, books are a kind of light," she says.

Ingrid does not sell books online, and she has no plans to. "If you want a book in two hours, you can order it from a big website," she says. "If you want a book that will change your life, come to Fjellvik and we'll talk about it." It is a philosophy that has made her one of the best-known booksellers in Norway – from the very end of the road.

(Vadbeno besedilo Učilnica.com)

  1. 0.Ingrid's bookshop is in a building that used to belong to ____.

  2. 1.Ingrid left Fjellvik at nineteen in order to ____.
  3. 2.At the publishing company, Ingrid's job included editing ____.
  4. 3.Ingrid realised that she never had time ____.
  5. 4.Ingrid's colleagues thought she would ____ the boathouse.
  6. 5.The shelves in the shop were made from ____.
  7. 6.The counter used to be ____.
  8. 7.In the first winter, Ingrid sometimes had no customers for ____.
  9. 8.The 'blind date' books had only a few words to ____.
  10. 9.The shop became popular with tourists after ____ wrote about it.
  11. 10.The books for the schoolchildren are paid for by ____.

naloge.besedilo:
Read the text and choose from the sentences below the one that fits each gap. Each sentence can be used only once. There are two extra sentences which you do not need to use. There is an example at the beginning: Gap 0 (G).

The truth about procrastination

Why do we delay the tasks we know we should do – and what can we do about it?

It is the night before an important deadline. You have known about the essay for weeks, but instead of writing it, you have tidied your room, answered every message and watched three episodes of a series. [0] If this sounds familiar, you are not alone: studies suggest that about one in five adults are chronic procrastinators.

For a long time, procrastination was seen as a problem of time management. [1] But psychologists now believe that this explanation misses the point. Most procrastinators know perfectly well how to plan; they simply do not follow their plans.

According to recent research, procrastination is really about emotions. [2] The task may be boring, difficult or frightening, or we may be afraid that the result will not be good enough. By putting it off, we escape these feelings – at least for a while.

The problem is that the relief does not last. [3] The task is still there, the deadline is closer, and now we also feel guilty. This creates a vicious circle: the worse we feel about a task, the more we want to avoid it.

Perfectionists are particularly at risk. [4] For them, it can feel safer not to start at all than to start and fail. A half-finished essay written at three in the morning at least comes with an excuse.

Our brains do not help either. [5] When we imagine ourselves in the future, brain scans show that we think about that person almost as if they were a stranger. So we happily leave the difficult work to "future me", who, we assume, will have more time and energy.

The good news is that there are strategies that work. [6] Telling yourself "I'll just write for ten minutes" is much less frightening than "I have to write the whole essay", and once people start, they often continue.

Another useful technique is to make the task less unpleasant. [7] Some people work in a café, listen to music or reward themselves with a short break after each part of the job.

Perhaps most surprisingly, research shows that being kind to yourself helps. [8] Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next one.

Finally, it is worth remembering that procrastination is not always bad. [9] Some creative people say that their best ideas come to them while they are doing something else. The trick is to know the difference between giving an idea time to grow and simply running away from it. [10]

(Vadbeno besedilo Učilnica.com)

  1. APeople were told to make lists, set priorities and use a diary.
  2. BWe delay a task because it makes us feel bad.
  3. CAs soon as we stop avoiding the task, the bad feelings return, often stronger than before.
  4. DThey set themselves such high standards that any task becomes a threat.
  5. EWe are naturally designed to prefer a reward now to a bigger one later.
  6. FOne of the simplest is to make the first step as small as possible.
  7. GNow it is midnight, and you have still not written a word.
  8. HWorking with a friend, for example, can turn a boring job into a social one.
  9. ICriticising yourself, on the other hand, only increases the stress that caused the problem.
  10. JSometimes a short delay gives our minds time to solve a problem in the background.
  11. KAnd that is a lesson worth learning sooner rather than later.
  12. LMost procrastinators are simply lazy and do not care about their work.
  13. MThis is why experts recommend that students should work through the night.
naloge.rezultat:
1. A
2. B
3. C
4. D
5. E
6. F
7. H
8. I
9. J
10. K
naloge.razlaga:
Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take
  • Kaj zahteva naloga: v vsako vrzel vstaviti en del povedi (ali poved). Dva dela sta odveč.
  • Postopek: preberi besedilo pred vrzeljo in za njo. Ugotovi, kaj mora slediti slovnično (oziralni zaimek, nedoločnik, veznik) in pomensko (razlog, nasprotje, posledica).
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: pravilen del se slovnično nadaljuje (npr. za samostalnikom kraja sledi »where …«, za »so« pa »that …«) in pomensko poveže misel pred vrzeljo in za njo.
  • Preverjanje: ko vstaviš vse dele, preberi celo besedilo; ostala dva dela ne smeta pasati nikamor.

Spodaj je pri vsaki postavki rešitev in razlaga, ki pokaže, kje v besedilu ali posnetku je odgovor in katero pravilo velja.

1. A
»a problem of time management« – A opiše tedanje nasvete (seznami, prioritete, dnevnik); sledi »But psychologists now believe …«.
2. B
»procrastination is really about emotions« – B to razloži; sledijo razlogi, zakaj je naloga neprijetna.
3. C
»the relief does not last« – C: slabi občutki se vrnejo; naslednja poved: naloga je še vedno tu, dodana je krivda.
4. D
»Perfectionists are particularly at risk« – D razloži zakaj; »For them« se nanaša na perfekcioniste.
5. E
»Our brains do not help either« – E: možgani raje izberejo nagrado zdaj; sledi razlaga o »future me«.
6. F
»strategies that work« – F uvede prvo (»One of the simplest«); sledi primer z desetimi minutami.
7. H
»make the task less unpleasant« – H poda primer (delo s prijateljem); sledijo drugi primeri (»Some people …«).
8. I
»being kind to yourself helps« – I poda nasprotje (samokritika poveča stres); sledi raziskava o odpuščanju.
9. J
»procrastination is not always bad« – J razloži, kdaj je odlog koristen; sledijo ustvarjalni ljudje.
10. K
Zaključek besedila: »sooner rather than later« – duhovita besedna igra s temo odlašanja.

The road that connected the world

The Silk Road was not a single road (0) a vast network of trade routes that connected China with the Mediterranean for more than fifteen hundred years. It got its name in the nineteenth century from a German geographer, (1) chose it because silk was one of the most valuable goods transported along it.

The routes began to develop in the second century BC, when the Chinese Han dynasty sent officials westwards to look (2) allies and horses. Soon caravans of camels were carrying silk, tea and porcelain across deserts and mountains, while gold, glass and wool travelled in the opposite direction. Very (3) traders made the whole journey. Instead, goods passed from merchant to merchant, and their price rose at every stage.

Travelling along the Silk Road was extremely dangerous. Merchants had to cross the Taklamakan Desert, whose name is often said to mean "you go in, but you do not come (4)", as well as some of the highest mountain passes in the world. They were also in constant danger of being attacked (5) bandits. To protect themselves, they travelled in large groups and rested in caravanserais, roadside inns (6) people and animals could spend the night safely.

However, the Silk Road was much more (7) a trade route. Along with goods, travellers carried ideas, religions and inventions. Buddhism spread from India to China along these routes, and paper, gunpowder and the compass travelled (8) east to west. Languages, music and recipes were exchanged too. Some historians believe that noodles and pasta may have a common origin in these contacts, (9) this is still disputed.

Not everything that travelled along the Silk Road was positive. In the fourteenth century, the plague known as the Black Death is thought to have spread from Central Asia to Europe partly (10) trade routes, killing perhaps a third of Europe's population.

The most famous traveller on the Silk Road was probably the Venetian merchant Marco Polo, who claimed to have spent seventeen years in China at the court of Kublai Khan. His book about his travels became extremely popular, (11) some readers did not believe a word of it.

The importance of the Silk Road declined in the fifteenth century, (12) European sailors discovered sea routes to Asia. Ships could carry far more goods than camels, and they did not have to pay taxes at every city (13) the way.

Today, the idea of the Silk Road has returned. China is investing huge sums in railways, roads and ports to connect Asia, Africa and Europe, a project often called the "New Silk Road". Whether it will bring the same exchange of ideas (14) the old one remains to be seen. But the original Silk Road reminds us that the world has been connected for much longer (15) we sometimes think – and that trade has always been about people as much (16) about goods.

naloge.razlaga:
Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take
  • Kaj zahteva naloga: v vsako vrzel napisati eno besedo. Navadno manjkajo slovnične besede: členi (a, the), predlogi (in, on, at), vezniki (although, because), oziralni zaimki (who, which, that), pomožni glagoli (have, is, did), primerjave (as, than).
  • Postopek: preberi celo poved; ugotovi, katera besedna vrsta manjka. Nato preveri ustaljene zveze (depend on, used to, as … as).
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: razlaga pove slovnično pravilo ali ustaljeno zvezo, ki zahteva prav to besedo. Kjer je več pravilnih rešitev, so navedene vse (ločene s poševnico).
  • Pasti: dve besedi v eni vrzeli; beseda, ki se pomensko ujema, a slovnično ne (who za stvari, that za vejico).

Spodaj je pri vsaki postavki rešitev in razlaga, ki pokaže, kje v besedilu ali posnetku je odgovor in katero pravilo velja.

1. who

2. for
»look for« = iskati.
3. few
»Very few traders« = zelo malo trgovcev (števni samostalnik).
4. out
»you go in, but you do not come out« – nasprotje in/out.
5. by
Vršilec dejanja v trpniku: attacked by bandits.
6. where
Oziralni prislov za kraj (inns).
7. than
»much more than a trade route« = veliko več kot.
8. from
»from east to west« = od vzhoda proti zahodu.
9. although / though / but
Dopustni veznik: although this is still disputed.
10. along / via / through
Kuga se je širila po trgovskih poteh: along trade routes.
11. although / though / but / even if
Nasprotje: priljubljena, čeprav ji nekateri niso verjeli.
12. when / after / as
Časovni veznik: when European sailors discovered sea routes.
13. on / along
Stalna zveza »on the way« = na poti.
14. as
»the same … as« = enak kot.
15. than
Primerjava: much longer than we think.
16. as
»as much as« = prav tako kot.

The dangerous power of political language

In recent years, many observers have noticed a worrying change in the way politicians speak. Instead of discussing ideas, they increasingly describe their opponents as enemies, traitors or even (0) (CRIME). This kind of language, experts warn, can have serious (1) (CONSEQUENT) for society.

Political debate has never been completely (2) (PEACE). Parliamentarians have always argued, and (3) (CRITICISE) of the government is an essential part of any democracy. But researchers who study political speeches say that the tone has become much more (4) (AGGRESSION) over the past two decades. Insults that would once have ended a career are now repeated on television and shared millions of times online.

Social media plays an important role in this (5) (DEVELOP). Posts that provoke strong emotions, especially anger and fear, spread faster than calm and balanced ones. Politicians know this, and some deliberately use (6) (PROVOKE) statements to attract attention. In this way, the most extreme voices often become the most visible.

The effects can be seen in the way citizens view each other. Surveys in several countries show that people are increasingly (7) (WILLING) to have friends with different political views, and some would even be unhappy if a member of their family married a supporter of another party. This growing (8) (DIVIDE) makes it harder to find compromises on important issues such as health care, education or climate change.

There is also a risk of (9) (VIOLENT). When leaders describe certain groups as a threat, some of their supporters may feel that attacks on those groups are (10) (JUSTIFY). Several studies have found a link between hostile political language and an increase in hate crimes.

Not everyone agrees that the situation is so (11) (DRAMA). Some argue that strong language is simply a sign of passionate debate and that voters are able to distinguish between rhetoric and reality. Others point out that (12) (RESTRICT) on political speech could be more dangerous than the problem itself.

Most experts agree, however, that politicians have a special (13) (RESPONSIBLE). Their words are heard by millions of people, and they help to decide what is considered acceptable. As one historian put it: "Democracy depends not only on free speech, but on the willingness to listen." Perhaps the first step is to remember that a political opponent is not an enemy, but simply someone who sees the world (14) (DIFFERENT).

Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take
  • Kaj zahteva naloga: besedo v oklepaju spremeniti tako, da se slovnično in pomensko prilega vrzeli (besedotvorje).
  • Postopek: 1) ugotovi, katera besedna vrsta manjka: za členom ali svojilnim zaimkom (the, its) samostalnik; pred samostalnikom pridevnik; ob glagolu ali pridevniku prislov; 2) preveri, ali je potrebna nikalna predpona (un-, in-, ir-, dis-) ali množina.

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to an interview with Sara Lindqvist, who started a natural skincare company at her kitchen table. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Sara, your company now sells skincare products in fourteen countries. But it all started in a kitchen, didn't it?

Sara: It did – a very small kitchen in a student flat in Edinburgh. I was studying chemistry, and I had terrible problems with my skin. Every cream I bought from the chemist's made it worse. So one evening I thought, I'm a chemistry student, why don't I make my own?

Interviewer: What did you use?

Sara: Very simple things at first: oats, honey, olive oil and a little beeswax that I bought from a farmer at the weekend market. My flatmates complained that the whole flat smelled like breakfast. But after three weeks my skin was better than it had been for years.

Interviewer: When did you realise it could become a business?

Sara: Honestly, I didn't plan it. I gave a few jars to friends as birthday presents, and then their friends started asking for them. By the end of my second year, I was selling about fifty jars a month, mostly through social media. I kept the money in a biscuit tin under my bed.

Interviewer: That's a long way from fourteen countries.

Sara: It is. The real turning point came when I finished university. I had a job offer from a big pharmaceutical company, with a good salary, and my parents were very keen for me to take it. Instead, I borrowed four thousand pounds from my grandmother and rented a tiny unit on an industrial estate. My parents thought I'd gone mad.

Interviewer: Were they right?

Sara: For the first year, it certainly looked like it. I made every mistake possible. Once I ordered two thousand glass jars and they arrived with the wrong lids. Another time a whole batch of cream went off because the unit got too hot in summer. I worked seven days a week and paid myself almost nothing. There were nights when I cried in the car park.

Interviewer: What kept you going?

Sara: The customers, really. People wrote to me – real letters, sometimes – saying that my cream had helped their child's eczema or that they finally felt comfortable in their own skin. You can't give up when you read something like that.

Interviewer: And then came the big break.

Sara: Yes. A well-known beauty journalist bought one of our creams in a little shop in the Highlands and wrote about it in a national newspaper. The next morning our website crashed. We received more orders in one weekend than in the whole previous year. I had to ask my mum, my aunt and two neighbours to help me pack boxes.

Interviewer: So your parents changed their minds?

Sara: My mum now works for the company three days a week! She's in charge of customer letters, because she says I'm too slow at answering them.

Interviewer: What's important to you now that the company is bigger?

Sara: That we don't forget where we started. We still use mostly local ingredients, all our packaging can be recycled, and we never test on animals. And every new product is still tested first in a kitchen – my own.

Interviewer: What advice would you give to young people who want to start a business?

Sara: Start small and start now. Don't wait until you have a perfect plan, because you never will. And keep your day costs low – I didn't buy a new car or a fancy office for six years.

Interviewer: Sara, thank you very much.

Sara: Thank you.

A young entrepreneur

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to a conversation with Tom Haddon and Elena Ruiz, who run a repair café in Bristol. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Presenter: In today's programme, we're talking about repair cafés – places where people bring broken things and volunteers help them fix them for free. With me are Tom Haddon and Elena Ruiz, who run one in Bristol. Tom, what exactly happens at a repair café?

Tom: Once a month, on the first Saturday, we take over a church hall for four hours. People arrive with whatever is broken – toasters, lamps, bicycles, jumpers with holes, even children's toys – and they sit down with one of our volunteers. The important thing is that we don't just repair things for people. They sit next to the volunteer and learn how to do it themselves.

Presenter: Elena, how did you get involved?

Elena: By accident, really. My grandmother's sewing machine stopped working, and every shop I went to told me it was too old to repair and that I should buy a new one. A friend told me about the repair café, so I went along. A retired engineer called Frank opened it up, found a tiny broken spring and fixed it in twenty minutes. I was so impressed that I signed up as a volunteer the same day.

Presenter: And now you run the café together.

Elena: Yes, for the last three years. Tom does the organising and I'm in charge of the textiles table – clothes, curtains, bags, that kind of thing.

Presenter: Tom, who are your volunteers?

Tom: All kinds of people. Many of them are retired – electricians, engineers, tailors – who have a lifetime of skills and want to use them. But we also have students, and one of our best bicycle mechanics is only fifteen. What they share is that they hate throwing things away.

Presenter: What are the most common repairs?

Tom: Electrical items, definitely. Vacuum cleaners, hair dryers, coffee machines. Very often the problem is something simple, like a loose wire or a blown fuse. Last year we kept a record and found that we managed to repair about two thirds of everything people brought in.

Presenter: And the other third?

Tom: Sometimes we can't get the spare part, or the product has been designed so that you can't open it without breaking it. That's one of our biggest frustrations. Some manufacturers glue their products together so that you can't change a battery, for example.

Elena: Which is why we also campaign for what's called the "right to repair" – laws that make companies sell spare parts and provide repair manuals. Things are starting to change, but slowly.

Presenter: Is it really about the environment, or is it about saving money?

Elena: Both, but I'd say it's also about community. People come for a repair and stay for the tea and cake. We have customers who come every month even when they've got nothing broken, just to chat. For some older people who live alone, it's the only social event in their month.

Tom: And there's something very satisfying about it. People arrive looking worried, holding a broken lamp that belonged to their mother, and they leave smiling. You can't buy that feeling in a shop.

Presenter: What would you say to someone who wants to start a repair café in their town?

Tom: Find a free space, a few people with skills, and a lot of tea. You don't need much money. And make sure you have insurance – that's the boring but important part.

Elena: And don't be afraid of not knowing everything. Half the time we learn together with the customer. I couldn't fix anything when I started.

Presenter: Tom, Elena, thank you very much.

Repair cafés

Report

Last year, the Green Schools Network, an organisation that supports environmental projects in European schools, started a two-year project called Our Sustainable School. Your school's Environmental Club decided to take part. During the past year, the club has carried out several activities to answer the following questions:

  • How do students and staff travel to school, and what could be improved?
  • How much energy and water does the school use, and how is it being reduced?
  • How is food waste in the school canteen dealt with?
To: Green Schools Network
From: Ana Kovač, Environmental Club
Subject: Our Sustainable School – findings after one year
naloge.rezultat: Formalno poročilo z glavo, uvodom z namenom, odstavki s podnaslovi za vsa tri vprašanja (prevoz v šolo, energija in voda, odpadna hrana) s podatki in ukrepi ter sklepom s priporočilom; 150–180 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Report (150–180 words), formal style
  2. How do students and staff travel to school, and what could be improved?
  3. How much energy and water does the school use, and how is it being reduced?
  4. How is food waste in the school canteen dealt with?
Kako napišeš poročilo (report)
Poročilo (report): zgradba
  • Glava: To: (komu) / From: (od koga) / Subject: (zadeva) / Date: (po želji). Nagovora »Dear …« ni.
  • Naslov ali kratek uvod z namenom: The aim/purpose of this report is to … / This report summarises …
  • Odstavki s podnaslovi: vsaka iztočnica dobi svoj odstavek z jasnim podnaslovom (Host family, School, Recommendations).
  • Sklep ali priporočila: Overall, … / I would recommend … / It would be a good idea to …
Slog poročila
  • Formalen, stvaren, jedrnat: dejstva, številke, ocene z utemeljitvijo.
  • Pogosti so trpnik in neosebni izrazi: The event was attended by … / It was felt that … / Most participants agreed that …
  • Ocena naj bo uravnotežena: pohvala in kritika (The timetable was well organised; however, …).
  • Ni skrajšanih oblik, ni čustvenih vzklikov. Prva oseba (I, we) je dovoljena, a besedilo naj ne zveni kot dnevnik.
Uporabne zveze
  • The aim of this report is to … · This report is based on …
  • The most successful part was … because … · One drawback was …
  • I would strongly recommend … · In conclusion, … · To sum up, …
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Zgradba poročila
To: Green Schools Network / From: Ana Kovač, Environmental Club / Subject: Our Sustainable School – findings after one year
Glava; naslov poročila.
Introduction – This report presents the findings of our club's research during the first year of the project.
Uvod z namenom; formalni slog.
Travelling to school
Survey of 600 students: 45 % come by car; suggestions: more bike racks, a walking bus.
Iztočnica 1: podatki iz raziskave + predlog.
Energy and water
LED lights in classrooms, switch-off monitors, water-saving taps; energy use down by 12 %.
Iztočnica 2: konkretni ukrepi in rezultati.
Food waste
We weighed leftovers for two weeks; smaller portions on request and a compost bin for the school garden.
Iztočnica 3: ugotovitev in ukrep.
Conclusion and recommendation – We have made good progress, but transport remains the biggest challenge.
Sklep s priporočilom.
Višja raven: natančni podatki, pasivne oblike (was carried out), pestro besedišče. Preštej besede (150–180).
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
To: Green Schools Network
From: Ana Kovač, Environmental Club
Subject: Our Sustainable School – findings after one year

Introduction

This report presents the findings of our club's research during the first year of the Our Sustainable School project.

Travelling to school

A survey of 600 students and staff revealed that 45 per cent come by car, although most live less than three kilometres away. We have therefore asked the town council for more bike racks and plan to organise a "walking bus" for younger students.

Energy and water

LED lights have been installed in all classrooms, computer monitors are switched off automatically in the evening, and water-saving taps have been fitted. As a result, energy use has fallen by twelve per cent.

Food waste

For two weeks we weighed leftovers in the canteen and found that a third of the food was wasted. Students can now ask for smaller portions, and a compost bin supplies our school garden.

Conclusion

We have made good progress, but transport remains our biggest challenge, so we recommend focusing on it next year.

Kako napišeš esej o književnem delu
Esej o književnem delu: zgradba
  • Uvod: avtor, naslov in teza, ki neposredno odgovori na navodilo (Will Freeman changes from a selfish man into …). Brez življenjepisa avtorja.
  • Jedro: dva do trije odstavki, vsak z eno trditvijo. Vsako trditev podpri s konkretnim prizorom ali kratkim navedkom in razloži, kaj pokaže (to je analiza).

  • Sklep: vrni se k tezi in pokaži, kaj pove o delu kot celoti.
Analiza namesto obnove
  • Navodilo pravi »Do not write about the text and/or the author in general«: ne obnavljaj zgodbe in ne piši splošno o avtorju.
  • Zgradba odstavka PEA: Point (trditev) → Evidence (prizor, navedek) → Analysis (kaj to pomeni za temo).
  • Uporabljaj sedanjik za dogajanje v delu (Will lies to the single mothers …).
  • Glagoli za analizo: shows, suggests, reveals, highlights, emphasises, symbolises.

  • This is evident when … · A turning point comes when … · This scene suggests that …
  • At the beginning of the novel, … By the end, … · Gradually, …
  • Whereas X …, Y … · Both novels show … · Unlike …, …

  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Načrt eseja
Uvod: teza – Boxer represents the loyal, hard-working working class, whose strength builds the revolution but whose blind trust allows the pigs to exploit it.
Teza v uvodu, brez obnove.
Jedro 1 – strength and loyalty: the strongest animal; his mottoes 'I will work harder' and 'Napoleon is always right'; he builds the windmill almost alone.
Ključni citati in prizori.
Jedro 2 – courage and kindness: hero of the Battle of the Cowshed, but sorry when he thinks he has killed a stable boy; he cannot learn the alphabet beyond D.
Pokaži dobroto in omejenost.
Jedro 3 – betrayal: when he collapses, the pigs sell him to the knacker; Squealer lies that he died in hospital; the pigs buy whisky.
Vrhunec izdaje.
Sklep: Boxer's fate shows that loyalty without critical thinking makes ordinary people victims of those in power.
Sklep razširi tezo.
Merila: vsebina in interpretacija, zgradba, jezik. 250–300 besed.
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
The role of Boxer in Animal Farm

In George Orwell's Animal Farm, Boxer the cart-horse is the most sympathetic character. He represents the loyal, hard-working working class: his strength makes the revolution possible, but his blind trust in the leaders allows the pigs to exploit him and, in the end, to destroy him.

From the beginning, Boxer is the strongest animal on the farm, and he is completely devoted to the cause. Whenever there is a problem, his answer is the same: "I will work harder!" He gets up earlier than everyone else and drags huge stones for the windmill. Later, he adds a second motto, "Napoleon is always right", which shows that he has given up thinking for himself.

Boxer is also brave and kind. He is the hero of the Battle of the Cowshed, yet when he believes he has killed a stable boy, he is genuinely sorry. However, he is not intelligent: he never learns the alphabet beyond the letter D. Because he cannot read the changing commandments, he accepts whatever Squealer tells him, even when he feels that something is wrong.

The cruelty of the pigs becomes clearest at the end of Boxer's life. When he collapses from overwork, Napoleon promises to send him to a hospital, but the van that takes him away belongs to a horse slaughterer. Squealer later claims that Boxer died peacefully in hospital, and soon afterwards the pigs obtain money to buy a case of whisky. The animal who gave everything to the farm is sold for the profit of its rulers.

In conclusion, Boxer's tragic fate is one of the strongest warnings in the novel. Orwell shows that loyalty and hard work without critical thinking turn ordinary people into victims of those in power.

Število besed: 294 (zahtevanih 250–300). Zgled je eden od mogočih odgovorov; tvoje besedilo je lahko drugačno, a mora izpolniti vse zahteve iz navodila.

Alone on the Ocean

When Emma Hart sailed into Plymouth harbour on a grey morning in June, hundreds of people were waiting on the quay. Some were waving flags, others were crying. Emma, who was just eighteen, had sailed around the world alone, without stopping, in a boat that was only eleven metres long. The journey had taken her two hundred and sixty-three days.

Emma grew up in a small fishing village in Cornwall, where her father repaired boats. She learned to sail at the age of six in a tiny wooden dinghy that he had built for her. "Other children had bicycles," she says. "I had a boat." By the age of twelve, she was competing in local races, and at fifteen she sailed across the English Channel to France with her father.

The idea of sailing around the world came to her after she read a book about the first people to do it alone. At first, her parents refused to take her seriously. It was only when she had saved enough money for the boat herself, by working in a café every weekend for three years, that they agreed to help her.

Preparing for the trip took two years. Emma had to learn how to repair the engine, sew sails and treat her own injuries. She also spent many hours with a psychologist, because being alone for months can be as dangerous for the mind as storms are for the boat. "The loneliness was the thing everyone worried about," she says. "But in fact I was never really lonely. I was too busy."

The hardest part of the journey was the Southern Ocean, near Antarctica. For three weeks, Emma sailed through storms with waves as high as a house. Once, her boat was knocked over by a huge wave, and the mast touched the water. "I was sure it was the end," she remembers. "But the boat came back up, and so did I."

During the long weeks at sea, Emma kept a blog, which she wrote on a satellite phone. Thousands of people followed her journey, and many schoolchildren sent her messages. She answered as many of them as she could. Her favourite message came from a nine-year-old girl who wrote: "When I grow up, I want to be brave like you."

Emma does not see herself as brave. "Brave people are those who feel afraid and do it anyway," she says. "I was afraid many times. But I also knew that I had prepared as well as I could."

Since her return, Emma has written a book about her journey and visits schools to talk about her experience. She now wants to start a sailing club for young people from poor families who would never normally have the chance to go to sea.

You will listen to an interview with Hannah Brooks, a volunteer with a mountain rescue team in the Lake District. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Hannah, you've been a mountain rescue volunteer for eleven years. What does the job involve?

Hannah: Well, first of all, it isn't a job – nobody in our team is paid. We're all volunteers with ordinary jobs. I'm a primary school teacher. But when the phone goes, day or night, we drop everything and go up the mountain to find people who are lost or injured.

Interviewer: How often does the phone go?

Hannah: Our team gets about a hundred and twenty call-outs a year. In summer it can be three or four in a single weekend. Most of them are walkers who have slipped and hurt an ankle, but we also look for people who are lost in fog, and sometimes climbers who have fallen.

Interviewer: How did you get involved?

Hannah: It was because of my dad. When I was fourteen, he broke his leg on a walk in the mountains, and a rescue team carried him down in the dark through the rain. It took them five hours. I remember sitting in the car park watching their lights coming down the hill, and I thought, I want to do that one day.

Interviewer: Was it difficult to join?

Hannah: Quite difficult, yes. You need to be very fit, of course, and you need a lot of experience in the mountains. Then there's a probation period of about a year, when you train with the team every Wednesday evening and one weekend a month. You learn first aid, navigation, how to use ropes, how to carry a stretcher across rocks. Only after that do you become a full member.

Interviewer: What's the hardest part?

Hannah: Physically, carrying a stretcher. A person on a stretcher, with all the equipment, can weigh well over a hundred kilos, and we sometimes carry them for hours. But emotionally, the hardest moments are when we arrive too late. Those days stay with you. We talk about them as a team afterwards, which really helps.

Interviewer: Has the job changed during your time with the team?

Hannah: Enormously. When I started, we used paper maps and radios. Now we use drones with thermal cameras, which can find a person in the dark by their body heat. And most people carry a mobile phone, so we can often find their location very quickly. Strangely, though, phones have also brought more call-outs.

Interviewer: Why is that?

Hannah: Because people rely on them too much. They follow a route on an app, the battery dies, and they have no map, no torch and no idea where they are. Or they go up in trainers and a T-shirt because the weather was nice in the valley. The weather in the mountains can change in minutes.

Interviewer: So what's your advice to walkers?

Hannah: Check the forecast, tell someone where you're going, and always carry a paper map, a torch, warm clothes and some food – even on a short walk. And don't be embarrassed to turn back. The mountain will still be there next week.

Interviewer: Do you ever think about giving up?

Hannah: Sometimes, at three in the morning, when it's raining sideways. But then you find someone who has been lying on a cold hillside for hours, and you see their face when they realise they're going to be all right. There's no feeling like it.

Interviewer: Hannah, thank you very much.

A mountain rescue volunteer

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to an interview with Erik Sundqvist, who helps to build an ice hotel in northern Sweden every winter. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Erik, you build a hotel every year – and every spring it melts. Why?

Erik: That's exactly the beauty of it. Nothing lasts for ever, and this hotel reminds you of that. It's built in November, it opens in December, and by the end of April it has turned back into water and flowed into the river. Then the next year we start again, with a completely new design.

Interviewer: Where does the ice come from?

Erik: From the river right next to the hotel. In March, when the ice is at its thickest, we cut huge blocks out of the river – each one weighs about two tonnes – and keep them in a cold storage hall through the summer. River ice is perfect because it moves slowly while it freezes, so it's very clear, almost like glass.

Interviewer: How long does it take to build the hotel?

Erik: About six weeks. We start with a steel frame, spray it with a mixture of snow and ice that we call "snice", and when it has frozen hard, we take the frame away. Then the artists arrive.

Interviewer: Artists?

Erik: Yes, every year we invite artists from all over the world to design the special suites. Each room is a different work of art. Last year, one room looked like the inside of a whale, and another was full of ice flowers. The artists don't need to have worked with ice before – some of them are painters or architects who have never touched a chainsaw.

Interviewer: What is it like to sleep in an ice room?

Erik: People are always worried about the cold, but the temperature inside stays between minus five and minus eight degrees, whatever the weather outside. You sleep in a thermal sleeping bag on reindeer skins, and most guests are surprised how warm they are. The hardest part is getting out of the sleeping bag in the morning!

Interviewer: Do most guests stay more than one night?

Erik: No, usually just one. Most people spend one night in the ice and the rest of their stay in warm rooms nearby. One night is an adventure; three would be a challenge.

Interviewer: What about the environment? Isn't it a strange idea, building with ice when the climate is getting warmer?

Erik: It's a fair question. We see the changes ourselves – the river freezes later than it used to. But in recent years we have also built a part of the hotel that stays open all year. It's kept cold with energy from solar panels, so in summer the sun actually keeps the ice frozen.

Interviewer: What do you enjoy most about your work?

Erik: The silence. When you're working inside the hotel early in the morning, before the guests wake up, you can hear the ice moving, a kind of soft cracking. It feels as if the building is alive.

Building with ice

Report

During the summer holidays, you and your family went on a one-day guided kayaking tour of the Soča valley organised by a company called Emerald River Adventures. The international youth travel magazine Young Explorer invites young travellers to share their experiences with its readers.

Write a report of 120–150 words for Young Explorer magazine in which you

  • describe the tour and say whether it matched the company's advertisement,
  • comment on the guide and the safety equipment,
  • say whether you would recommend the tour to other young travellers and why.
To: Young Explorer magazine
From: Nika Zupan
Subject: Emerald River Adventures – kayaking tour
naloge.rezultat: Formalno poročilo z glavo, uvodom z namenom, odstavki s podnaslovi (opis izleta in primerjava z oglasom, vodnik in varnostna oprema, priporočilo z utemeljitvijo) in sklepom; 120–150 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Report (120–150 words), formal style
  2. describe the tour and say whether it matched the company's advertisement
  3. comment on the guide and the safety equipment
  4. say whether you would recommend the tour to other young travellers and why
Kako napišeš poročilo (report)
Poročilo (report): zgradba
  • Glava: To: (komu) / From: (od koga) / Subject: (zadeva) / Date: (po želji). Nagovora »Dear …« ni.
  • Naslov ali kratek uvod z namenom: The aim/purpose of this report is to … / This report summarises …
  • Odstavki s podnaslovi: vsaka iztočnica dobi svoj odstavek z jasnim podnaslovom (Host family, School, Recommendations).
  • Sklep ali priporočila: Overall, … / I would recommend … / It would be a good idea to …
Slog poročila
  • Formalen, stvaren, jedrnat: dejstva, številke, ocene z utemeljitvijo.
  • Pogosti so trpnik in neosebni izrazi: The event was attended by … / It was felt that … / Most participants agreed that …
  • Ocena naj bo uravnotežena: pohvala in kritika (The timetable was well organised; however, …).
  • Ni skrajšanih oblik, ni čustvenih vzklikov. Prva oseba (I, we) je dovoljena, a besedilo naj ne zveni kot dnevnik.
Uporabne zveze
  • The aim of this report is to … · This report is based on …
  • The most successful part was … because … · One drawback was …
  • I would strongly recommend … · In conclusion, … · To sum up, …
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Zgradba poročila

Iztočnica 2: pohvala in kritika.

To: Young Explorer magazine
From: Nika Zupan
Subject: Emerald River Adventures – kayaking tour

Introduction

The aim of this report is to describe the one-day kayaking tour of the Soča valley that my family took in August.

The tour

We spent six hours on the river and stopped for a picnic lunch on a beach. The scenery was breathtaking. However, the advertisement promised "small groups", but there were twenty people in ours.

Guide and safety

Our guide was friendly, spoke excellent English and explained everything clearly. The helmets and life jackets were new, although some wetsuits were too small.

Recommendation

I would recommend the tour to active young travellers, as it is exciting and reasonably priced. I would suggest booking in June, when groups are smaller.

Conclusion

Overall, it was an unforgettable day despite a few small problems.

Choose ONE essay title.

  1. Travelling is the best form of education.
  2. Smartphones should be banned in schools.

naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Choose ONE title and underline it.
  2. State clearly how far you agree or disagree.
  3. Support your opinion with arguments and examples.
  4. Write 220–250 words.
Kako napišeš argumentativni esej
Argumentativni esej: zgradba
  • Uvod (2–3 povedi): uvedi temo s splošno mislijo, trditev iz naslova povej s svojimi besedami in jasno zavzemi stališče (I largely agree that … / I am not convinced that …).
  • Jedro (2–3 odstavki): vsak odstavek ima en argument. Zgradba odstavka: temeljna poved (argument) → razlaga (zakaj drži) → konkreten primer (izkušnja, podatek, primer iz Slovenije).
  • Protiargument: v enem odstavku predstavi nasprotno mnenje in ga ovrzi (Critics argue that … However, …). To pokaže zrelost razmišljanja.
  • Sklep (2–3 povedi): povzemi stališče in odgovori na vprašanje »How far do you agree?«. Brez novih argumentov.
Kako dobiš točke za vsebino
  • Odgovori na naslov, ki si ga izbral, in ga podčrtaj. Ne piši o drugem naslovu.
  • Stališče naj bo jasno in dosledno od uvoda do sklepa. »Deloma se strinjam« je dovoljeno, če pojasniš, v čem da in v čem ne.
  • Primeri morajo biti konkretni: »My cousin spent a year in Ghana …« je boljše kot »Many people do it«.
Uporabne zveze
  • Mnenje: In my opinion, … · I firmly believe that … · It seems to me that …
  • Dodajanje: Furthermore, … · What is more, … · In addition, …
  • Nasprotje: However, … · On the other hand, … · Although …, … · Critics argue that …
  • Primer: For example, … · For instance, … · A good example of this is …
  • Sklep: All things considered, … · To sum up, … · In conclusion, …
Pogoste napake
  • Uvod, ki dobesedno prepiše naslov.
  • Argument brez primera ali primer brez povezave z argumentom.
  • Neformalen slog: you know, a lot of, kids, skrajšane oblike.
  • Prekratko jedro in predolg uvod.
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Načrt (velja za oba naslova)
Uvod: preoblikuj trditev in povej stališče (I largely agree that travelling teaches us things no classroom can …).
Teza v uvodu.
Jedro 1: argument + primer (languages, other cultures, an exchange trip).
Konkretni primeri.
Jedro 2: argument + primer (independence, solving problems on your own).
Povezovalci.
Jedro 3: protiargument (travel is expensive; it cannot replace systematic knowledge … However …).
Uravnoteženost.
Sklep: povzemi stališče.
Brez novih argumentov.
Ideje za 2. naslov
For: distraction, cyberbullying, less face-to-face contact. Against: useful for research, emergencies, learning apps; better to teach responsible use.
Izberi en naslov in ga podčrtaj.
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
Travelling is the best form of education.

Last spring, I spent two weeks with a host family in Ireland on a school exchange. In those two weeks I learned more English, and more about myself, than in a whole year of lessons. That is why I largely agree that travelling is the best form of education, even though it cannot replace school completely.

Firstly, travelling teaches us about other cultures in a way no textbook can. When you eat dinner with a family abroad, listen to their opinions and follow their customs, you begin to understand that there are many ways of living. This makes people more tolerant and open-minded.

Secondly, travel makes us independent. On a trip, we have to read timetables, ask strangers for directions, deal with money in another currency and solve unexpected problems, such as a missed train. These practical skills are rarely taught in the classroom, but they are essential in adult life.

On the other hand, travelling has its limits. It is expensive, so not everyone can afford it, and a short holiday on a beach teaches us very little. Moreover, subjects such as mathematics or chemistry require systematic study, which is difficult to replace with experience alone.

In conclusion, I believe that travelling is the most valuable form of education because it develops our understanding of the world and our independence. However, it works best together with school, not instead of it. Schools should therefore support more exchanges.

The world's most mysterious book

In 1912, a book dealer called Wilfrid Voynich bought a collection of old manuscripts from a Jesuit college near Rome. Among them was a small book, about the size of a modern paperback, that he could not understand. Neither could anyone else. More than a century later, the book that now carries his name remains one of the greatest puzzles in the history of writing.

The Voynich manuscript has around 240 pages, written in an elegant, flowing script that does not match any known language. Almost every page is decorated with colourful drawings. Some show plants that botanists have never been able to identify. Others show circular diagrams of stars and planets, and a whole section is filled with pictures of small women bathing in green and blue pools connected by strange pipes.

For a long time, many experts believed that the book was a clever fake, perhaps made by Voynich himself to sell at a high price. This theory became much harder to support in 2009, when scientists at the University of Arizona carried out radiocarbon dating on the parchment. The tests showed that it had been made in the early fifteenth century. The ink is thought to be of similar age, although the parchment could in theory have been written on later.

Some of the book's history is known. A letter found with the manuscript claims that it was once bought by the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II, a famous collector of curiosities, for the huge sum of 600 gold coins. It later passed through the hands of several scholars in Prague before disappearing for about two hundred years.

Over the decades, the manuscript has attracted codebreakers of every kind. During and after the Second World War, some of the American cryptographers who had broken Japanese codes spent years trying to read it, without success. In recent years, linguists and computer scientists have used artificial intelligence to analyse the text. Their results show that the script has patterns similar to those of real languages: some "words" appear much more often than others, just as "the" and "and" do in English.

Every few years, someone announces that they have finally solved the mystery. It has been described as an early form of Turkish, a medical handbook written in a lost dialect, and even a message from another world. So far, none of these solutions has convinced the experts.

Today, the manuscript is kept in a library at Yale University in the United States, where it is protected in a climate-controlled room. Anyone can see it, however: the whole book has been photographed and put online, and thousands of amateur researchers study it every day. Perhaps one of them will one day succeed where the experts have failed. Or perhaps, as some believe, the book was never meant to be read at all.
