Discuss the role of Squealer in George Orwell's Animal Farm.

George Orwell: Animal Farm

Write an essay of 250–300 words. Do not write about the text and/or the author in general.
naloge.rezultat: Esej s tezo o Squealerju kot propagandnem stroju, podprto s prizori (mleko in jabolka, Snowball kot izdajalec, izmišljene statistike, spreminjanje zapovedi in prizor z lestvijo, laž o Boxerjevi smrti); brez obnove; 250–300 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Discuss the role of Squealer in George Orwell's Animal Farm.
  2. Do not write about the text and/or the author in general (no plot summary, no biography).
  3. Write 250–300 words.
Kako napišeš esej o književnem delu
Esej o književnem delu: zgradba
  • Uvod: avtor, naslov in teza, ki neposredno odgovori na navodilo (Will Freeman changes from a selfish man into …). Brez življenjepisa avtorja.
  • Jedro: dva do trije odstavki, vsak z eno trditvijo. Vsako trditev podpri s konkretnim prizorom ali kratkim navedkom in razloži, kaj pokaže (to je analiza).
  • Primerjava (če gre za dve deli): primerjaj neposredno z »Whereas …«, »Similarly, …«, »In contrast, …«, ne napiši dveh ločenih esejev.
  • Sklep: vrni se k tezi in pokaži, kaj pove o delu kot celoti.
Analiza namesto obnove
  • Navodilo pravi »Do not write about the text and/or the author in general«: ne obnavljaj zgodbe in ne piši splošno o avtorju.
  • Zgradba odstavka PEA: Point (trditev) → Evidence (prizor, navedek) → Analysis (kaj to pomeni za temo).
  • Uporabljaj sedanjik za dogajanje v delu (Will lies to the single mothers …).
  • Glagoli za analizo: shows, suggests, reveals, highlights, emphasises, symbolises.
Uporabne zveze
  • This is evident when … · A turning point comes when … · This scene suggests that …
  • At the beginning of the novel, … By the end, … · Gradually, …
  • Whereas X …, Y … · Both novels show … · Unlike …, …
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Načrt eseja
Uvod: teza – Squealer is Napoleon's propaganda machine; he shows that power depends not only on force but on controlling information.
Teza v uvodu, brez obnove.
Jedro 1 – the persuader: 'he could turn black into white'; he explains why the pigs need the milk and apples ('for your sake').
Prvi primer propagande.
Jedro 2 – rewriting history: Snowball becomes a traitor; the windmill was 'Napoleon's idea'; statistics show that food production has increased.
Laži in izmišljene številke.
Jedro 3 – changing the commandments: Squealer found at night next to the broken ladder and a pot of paint; Boxer's death explained as a peaceful death in hospital.
Vrhunec manipulacije.
Sklep: Squealer, with the dogs, keeps the animals obedient; Orwell warns that propaganda is as dangerous as violence.
Sklep se vrne k tezi.
Merila: vsebina in interpretacija, zgradba, jezik. 250–300 besed.
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
The role of Squealer in Animal Farm

In George Orwell's Animal Farm, Napoleon controls the farm with the help of his fierce dogs, but he also relies on a weapon that is less visible and perhaps even more powerful: Squealer. This clever, fat pig is Napoleon's propaganda machine, and his role shows that power depends not only on force but on controlling information.

From the start, Squealer is described as a brilliant talker; the other animals say that "he could turn black into white". His first important task is to explain why the pigs keep the milk and apples for themselves. Pigs need them for their brains, he claims, and they are taking them only for the sake of the other animals. If the pigs failed, he warns, Jones would come back – an argument that nobody dares to question.

As Napoleon's power grows, Squealer rewrites history. After Snowball is driven away, Squealer tells the animals that he was a traitor from the beginning and that the windmill was really Napoleon's idea. He also reads out long lists of figures proving that food production has increased, even though the animals are hungrier than ever.

Squealer's most cynical work concerns the Seven Commandments. One night he is found lying next to a broken ladder with a pot of white paint, and the next day a commandment has changed. Later, when Boxer is sold to the knacker, Squealer invents a touching story about his peaceful death in hospital.

In conclusion, Squealer represents the propaganda of totalitarian states, which makes people doubt their own memories. Orwell suggests that lies repeated often enough can be just as dangerous as violence, because they persuade victims to accept their own oppression.

Število besed: 284 (zahtevanih 250–300). Zgled je eden od mogočih odgovorov; tvoje besedilo je lahko drugačno, a mora izpolniti vse zahteve iz navodila.

The Long Walk Home

Three years ago, Daniel Price closed the door of his flat in Bristol, put on a rucksack and started walking. Fourteen months and nine thousand kilometres later, he arrived in Istanbul. He had crossed eleven countries on foot, worn out seven pairs of boots and, he says, learned more about people than in the whole of his previous life.

Daniel was thirty-two at the time and working in an insurance office. "I spent nine hours a day looking at a screen," he says. "One morning, sitting on a crowded train, I realised that I couldn't remember the last time I had seen a sunrise." That evening he bought a map of Europe and drew a line across it.

He planned to camp most nights, but in the end he spent more than half of the nights in people's homes. Strangers invited him in after seeing him on the road. In a village in northern France, a farmer let him sleep in his barn and then insisted that he stay for a family wedding the next day. In Hungary, a retired teacher walked with him for a whole week because she wanted to practise her English.

The journey was not always easy. In the Alps, Daniel was caught in a snowstorm and had to spend two nights in an empty mountain hut. In the summer, the heat in southern Europe was so intense that he could walk only in the early morning and late evening. He also had problems with his feet, and for a while in Croatia he could hardly walk at all.

The loneliness was harder than the physical difficulties. "There were days when I didn't speak to anyone," he says. "Then I'd talk to cows, to trees, to myself." To stay in touch with home, he wrote a short blog post every evening, and by the end of the journey it had more than fifty thousand readers.

Daniel carried very little: a tent, a sleeping bag, a few clothes, a small stove and a notebook. He did not use a phone for navigation, preferring paper maps, which he posted home when he had finished with them. Today, the maps cover one wall of his kitchen.

Since returning, Daniel has written a book about his walk and now works as a guide, leading small groups on long-distance hiking trips. He no longer owns a car. "When you have walked across a continent," he says, "you realise that you rarely need to go anywhere in a hurry."

  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: v razlagi spodaj je navedek iz besedila (v narekovajih), na katerem temelji odgovor. Odgovor je pravilen, če pove isto kot navedek, tudi s svojimi besedami.
  • Pasti: odgovor ima preveč besed (več kot 5 ni sprejemljivo); odgovor vsebuje dodatno napačno informacijo; prepišeš del besedila, ki ne odgovarja na vprašanje.

You will listen to an interview with Marco Bellini, a chef who runs a restaurant that produces almost no rubbish. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Marco, your restaurant in Leeds doesn't have a rubbish bin. Is that true?

Marco: It's true. We have a compost bin and a recycling box for glass, but no ordinary bin. Last year, all the rubbish we couldn't recycle or compost fitted into one small bucket.

Interviewer: How is that possible in a busy restaurant?

Marco: It starts with the suppliers. We buy almost everything from local farmers, and they deliver in reusable crates, not in plastic or cardboard. Our flour comes in big cloth sacks that we send back to the mill. Milk arrives in metal churns, like fifty years ago.

Interviewer: Where did the idea come from?

Marco: From my first job, in a hotel kitchen in London. I was nineteen, and at the end of every evening I had to carry huge bags of food waste out to the bins – whole trays of bread, vegetables, even meat that nobody had touched. One night I counted: we threw away more food than we served. I couldn't sleep after that.

Interviewer: So what do you do differently?

Marco: We use every part of everything. When we cook carrots, the tops become pesto. Stale bread becomes breadcrumbs or a pudding. The bones from the meat go into stock, and vegetable peelings are dried and turned into a powder that we use for seasoning. And what really can't be eaten goes into the compost, which goes back to the farms that grow our vegetables.

Interviewer: Doesn't that limit the menu?

Marco: It makes it more creative. We don't have a fixed menu – it changes every day, depending on what the farmers bring. Customers don't choose from a long list; there are just three dishes each evening. Some people found that strange at first, but now they come precisely because they don't know what they'll get.

Interviewer: What about the customers' leftovers?

Marco: We serve smaller portions, and if people are still hungry, they can have more for free. That simple change reduced plate waste by about seventy per cent. And if someone can't finish their meal, they can take it home in a jar – but they have to bring the jar back.

Interviewer: Is it more expensive to run a restaurant like this?

Marco: At first, yes. But now we actually save money, because we buy less and waste nothing. The hardest part is the time. Making everything ourselves – butter, bread, even our own cleaning products – takes many extra hours.

Interviewer: What would you say to people who want to waste less at home?

Marco: Plan your meals and shop with a list. Freeze things before they go bad. And learn to love leftovers – yesterday's dinner can be tomorrow's lunch.

A zero-waste chef

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to a conversation with historian Dr Clare Hughes and museum curator Sam Patel about the history of board games. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Presenter: With us today are historian Clare Hughes and Sam Patel, who has just opened an exhibition about board games. Clare, how old are board games?

Clare: Much older than most people think. One of the oldest we know is Senet, which was played in ancient Egypt about five thousand years ago. Boards have been found in the tombs of the pharaohs, including Tutankhamun's. The Egyptians believed the game was connected to the journey of the soul after death.

Presenter: So games weren't just for fun?

Clare: Often not. Many early games were connected with religion or used to predict the future. Others were used to teach strategy. Chess, for example, developed in India around the sixth century and was originally a kind of war game, with pieces representing infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots.

Presenter: Sam, what's the oldest object in your exhibition?

Sam: It's a set of dice made of bone, found in Turkey. They're about four thousand years old, but if you put them next to modern dice, you can hardly tell the difference. That's what I find so moving about games – people thousands of years ago enjoyed exactly the same tension when they rolled a dice.

Presenter: Are there any surprising stories in the exhibition?

Sam: Plenty. My favourite is about Monopoly. Most people think it was invented in the 1930s, but it's based on an earlier game called The Landlord's Game, designed by a woman named Elizabeth Magie in 1904. Her aim was actually to show how unfair it is when a few people own all the land. Ironically, the game became a celebration of getting rich.

Clare: There's another wonderful story from the Second World War. British intelligence produced special board game sets for prisoners of war. Hidden inside them were maps printed on silk, small compasses and real money, to help prisoners escape.

Presenter: Why do you think board games are so popular again today?

Sam: Sales have grown enormously in the last ten years. I think it's because people spend so much time looking at screens that they want to do something together, face to face. Board game cafés have opened in many cities, where you can order coffee and choose from hundreds of games.

Clare: And modern games are much more varied. In many of them, players don't compete against each other – they cooperate to beat the game itself. That's quite new.

Presenter: Sam, what do you hope visitors will take away from the exhibition?

Sam: That play isn't childish. It's one of the oldest things humans do together. And I hope they'll go home and get their old games out of the cupboard.

The history of board games

naloge.besedilo:
E-mail

VOLUNTEER ON A GREEK ISLAND THIS SUMMER
The Turtle Shore Project is looking for volunteers aged 18–25 to protect sea turtle nests, collect data on beaches and talk to tourists about conservation. Good English and teamwork skills are essential.
Contact: volunteers@turtleshore.org

You have seen the advertisement and have decided to apply. Write an e-mail of application of 120–150 words in which you:

  • explain why you are interested in the work,
  • describe the skills and qualities that make you suitable,
  • suggest how you could contribute to the team.
naloge.rezultat: Formalno e-pismo – prošnja za prostovoljno delo: formalni nagovor, uvod z namenom, razlogi za zanimanje, spretnosti in lastnosti, predlog prispevka k ekipi, formalen konec; 120–150 besed.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. E-mail (120–150 words), formal style
  2. explain why you are interested in the work
  3. describe the skills and qualities that make you suitable
  4. suggest how you could contribute to the team
Kako napišeš formalno e-pismo
Formalno e-pismo: zgradba
  • Nagovor: »Dear Mr Smith,« / »Dear Ms Novak,« (če poznaš ime) ali »Dear Sir or Madam,« (če ga ne poznaš). Za nagovorom vejica, nato nov odstavek z veliko začetnico.
  • Uvodni odstavek: v eni ali dveh povedih povej, zakaj pišeš (I am writing to complain about … / I am writing to apply for …).
  • Jedro: vsaka iztočnica v svojem odstavku, s konkretnimi podatki (datumi, številke, primeri).
  • Sklepni odstavek: kaj pričakuješ (I look forward to hearing from you. / I would be grateful if you could …).
  • Pozdrav: »Yours sincerely,« (če si začel z imenom), »Yours faithfully,« (če si začel z Dear Sir or Madam) ali nevtralno »Kind regards,«. Nato ime in priimek.
E-pismo s pritožbo (complaint)
  • Povej, kaj si kupil ali obiskal in kdaj (I ordered a pair of headphones on 3 May, order number …).
  • Opiši težave stvarno, eno za drugo, s posledicami (As a result, I had to …).
  • Izrazi nezadovoljstvo vljudno, a odločno: I was extremely disappointed … / This is not what your advertisement promised.
  • Zahtevaj rešitev: I would like a full refund / a replacement. I expect … within … days.
E-pismo s prijavo (application)
  • Povej, kje si videl oglas in za kaj se prijavljaš (I am writing to apply for the position of … advertised on your website).
  • Predstavi se in navedi izkušnje in znanja, ki ustrezajo oglasu (I have been volunteering … / I speak English and German fluently).
  • Pojasni, zakaj te delo zanima in kaj lahko ponudiš (I believe I would be a valuable member of your team because …).
  • Postavi vprašanje, če ga navodilo zahteva (I would also like to know whether accommodation is provided).
Uporabne zveze
  • I would be grateful if you could … · Could you please let me know …? · I would appreciate it if …
  • Firstly, … Secondly, … In addition, … Furthermore, … However, … Therefore, …
  • Please find attached my CV. · I am available for an interview at any time.
Pogoste napake
  • Nagovor »Hello« ali »Hi« in pozdrav »Bye« v formalnem pismu.
  • Skrajšane oblike (I'm, don't, can't) in pogovorni izrazi (gonna, stuff, really cool).
  • Ena dolga poved brez odstavkov; ena iztočnica omenjena le v pol povedi.
  • »Yours sincerely« za »Dear Sir or Madam« (pravilno je Yours faithfully).
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Dear Sir or Madam,
Formalni nagovor.
I am writing to apply for a place as a volunteer with the Turtle Shore Project.
Uvod z namenom pisma.
I am interested because I love the sea and want to study biology.
Iztočnica 1: razlog za zanimanje.
I am patient and reliable, I speak good English and I am used to working outdoors.
Iztočnica 2: spretnosti in lastnosti s primeri.
I could help by organising activities for children, taking photos for your website …
Iztočnica 3: konkreten prispevek.
I look forward to hearing from you. / Yours faithfully, / Luka Novak
Formalen konec.
Preštej besede (120–150).
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to apply for a place as a volunteer with the Turtle Shore Project, which I saw advertised online.

I am very interested in this work because I have loved the sea since I was a child, and I am planning to study marine biology at university. Protecting sea turtles would be a wonderful chance to gain practical experience.

I am patient, reliable and used to working outdoors in hot weather, as I have spent two summers helping on my uncle's farm. My English is good, and I can also speak some Italian, which could be useful when talking to tourists.

I enjoy working in a team and could contribute by organising activities for children on the beach or taking photographs for your website and social media.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Yours faithfully,
Luka Novak

Število besed: 144 (zahtevanih 120–150). Zgled je eden od mogočih odgovorov; tvoje besedilo je lahko drugačno, a mora izpolniti vse zahteve iz navodila.

Choose ONE essay title.

  1. Money can't buy happiness.
  2. Young people today depend on their parents for too long.

Underline the essay title you have chosen. How far do you agree or disagree with the statement? Support your opinion in 220–250 words.
naloge.rezultat: Argumentativni esej z jasnim stališčem, argumenti s primeri, protiargumentom in sklepom; 220–250 besed, en izbrani naslov.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Choose ONE title and underline it.
  2. State clearly how far you agree or disagree.
  3. Support your opinion with arguments and examples.
  4. Write 220–250 words.
Kako napišeš argumentativni esej
Argumentativni esej: zgradba
  • Uvod (2–3 povedi): uvedi temo s splošno mislijo, trditev iz naslova povej s svojimi besedami in jasno zavzemi stališče (I largely agree that … / I am not convinced that …).
  • Jedro (2–3 odstavki): vsak odstavek ima en argument. Zgradba odstavka: temeljna poved (argument) → razlaga (zakaj drži) → konkreten primer (izkušnja, podatek, primer iz Slovenije).
  • Protiargument: v enem odstavku predstavi nasprotno mnenje in ga ovrzi (Critics argue that … However, …). To pokaže zrelost razmišljanja.
  • Sklep (2–3 povedi): povzemi stališče in odgovori na vprašanje »How far do you agree?«. Brez novih argumentov.
Kako dobiš točke za vsebino
  • Odgovori na naslov, ki si ga izbral, in ga podčrtaj. Ne piši o drugem naslovu.
  • Stališče naj bo jasno in dosledno od uvoda do sklepa. »Deloma se strinjam« je dovoljeno, če pojasniš, v čem da in v čem ne.
  • Primeri morajo biti konkretni: »My cousin spent a year in Ghana …« je boljše kot »Many people do it«.
Uporabne zveze
  • Mnenje: In my opinion, … · I firmly believe that … · It seems to me that …
  • Dodajanje: Furthermore, … · What is more, … · In addition, …
  • Nasprotje: However, … · On the other hand, … · Although …, … · Critics argue that …
  • Primer: For example, … · For instance, … · A good example of this is …
  • Sklep: All things considered, … · To sum up, … · In conclusion, …
Pogoste napake
  • Uvod, ki dobesedno prepiše naslov.
  • Argument brez primera ali primer brez povezave z argumentom.
  • Neformalen slog: you know, a lot of, kids, skrajšane oblike.
  • Prekratko jedro in predolg uvod.
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Načrt (velja za oba naslova)
Uvod: preoblikuj trditev in povej stališče (I agree that money alone cannot make us happy, although …).
Teza v uvodu.
Jedro 1: argument + primer (rich people can be lonely; friendships and health matter more).
Konkretni primeri.
Jedro 2: argument + primer (experiences and relationships make us happier than things).
Povezovalci.
Jedro 3: protiargument (poverty causes stress; money buys security and opportunities … However …).
Uravnoteženost.
Sklep: povzemi stališče.
Brez novih argumentov.
Ideje za 2. naslov
For: living at home until 30, parents pay for everything. Against: expensive flats, long studies, temporary jobs; staying close to family is not always bad.
Izberi en naslov in ga podčrtaj.
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
Money can't buy happiness.

Lottery winners are often expected to live happily ever after, yet many of them say that their lives became more complicated after their win. I agree that money alone cannot buy happiness, although it certainly makes some things easier.

Firstly, the things that make us truly happy cannot be bought. Friendship, love and good health are far more important than an expensive car. A rich person who is lonely or ill is unlikely to be happier than someone with little money but a close family and good friends.

Secondly, research suggests that experiences make us happier than possessions. The excitement of a new phone fades after a few weeks, but memories of a camping trip with friends or a family celebration stay with us for years. Moreover, people who chase money often work so hard that they have no time to enjoy their lives.

On the other hand, it would be naive to say that money does not matter. Poverty causes enormous stress, and people who cannot afford food, housing or medical care find it very hard to be happy. Money also gives us security and opportunities, such as a good education. However, once our basic needs are met, more money does not seem to make us much happier.

In conclusion, I believe that money is important for a comfortable life, but it cannot guarantee happiness. In my opinion, it is relationships, health and meaningful experiences that make life worth living.

Read the text and answer the questions in note form in the spaces below. Use 1–5 words for each answer. All contracted forms with the exception of can’t count as two words. There is an example at the beginning: Answer 0.

The secret army of codebreakers

For more than thirty years after the end of the Second World War, thousands of British women kept a secret so well that not even their husbands or children knew about it. When they were asked what they had done during the war, they said they had worked in an office, or done some typing. In reality, they had been part of one of the most important operations of the war: breaking the secret codes of Nazi Germany.

The work took place at Bletchley Park, a country house about eighty kilometres north-west of London. When the war began, the British government brought together a small group of mathematicians, linguists and chess champions there. Their task was to read the messages that the German army, navy and air force sent using the Enigma machine, which changed its settings every day and was believed to be impossible to break.

As the war continued, the operation grew enormously. By 1945, almost ten thousand people worked at Bletchley Park, and about three quarters of them were women. Many were recruited straight from school or university, sometimes because they were good at crossword puzzles or spoke German. Others were chosen simply because they could be trusted to keep quiet.

Most of the women did hard, repetitive work. Some operated the "bombes", huge electro-mechanical machines that helped to find the daily Enigma settings. The machines were noisy and hot, and the women worked in shifts around the clock, including at night. Others typed out decoded messages, translated them or kept the enormous card indexes that helped analysts connect pieces of information.

A few women became codebreakers themselves. Mavis Lever, who had been studying German at university, was only nineteen when she broke a message that helped the British navy win a battle in the Mediterranean in 1941. Joan Clarke, a brilliant mathematician, worked closely with Alan Turing, although she was paid less than the men doing the same job.

Every person who worked at Bletchley Park had to sign the Official Secrets Act, and they took their promise extremely seriously. Many did not even tell colleagues in other huts what they were working on. It was only in the 1970s, when information about the codebreaking was officially made public, that they were free to talk – and by then many of them had died without ever telling their story.

Historians believe that the work at Bletchley Park shortened the war by up to two years and saved millions of lives. Today, the house is a museum, and the women who worked there have finally received recognition. In 2009, the British government created a special badge for all surviving veterans. Many of the women who received it were in their nineties. "We were just doing our job," one of them said. "We never thought anyone would want to know."

  11. 10.When were the workers free to talk about their work?
  12. 11.What did the government create in 2009?

naloge.besedilo:
Read the text and match the statements with the paragraphs. More than one statement may refer to the same paragraph. There is an example at the beginning: Example 0.

Life without …

Five people describe what happened when they gave up something most of us take for granted.

A Without a car – Helen, 45

We sold our car when it failed its safety test and we couldn't afford a new one. I expected it to be a temporary situation. Four years later, we still haven't bought one. We cycle to school and work, take the train to visit my parents and rent a car twice a year for holidays. The biggest surprise has been how much money we save – almost three thousand pounds a year. My children are fitter than their friends, although they still complain when it rains.

B Without a smartphone – Jakub, 19

I swapped my smartphone for an old phone that can only make calls and send texts. My friends thought I had lost my mind. At first, I kept reaching into my pocket for something that wasn't there, and I felt left out because I missed group chats. But after a month, I was sleeping better and reading again. The worst part is navigation – I've got lost more times than I can count. I've started carrying a paper map, which my friends find hilarious.

C Without a supermarket – Amira, 33

For one year, I promised to buy food only from markets, farms and small local shops. It took much longer to do the shopping, and in winter there was very little fresh fruit. But I got to know the people who grow my food, and I started cooking meals from scratch. I also produced far less packaging waste. I don't think I'll ever go back to shopping the way I did before, although I do sometimes miss being able to buy everything in one place.

D Without a television – Peter, 61

When our television broke ten years ago, we simply didn't replace it. My wife and I had always said we watched too much. Instead, we talk more – about books, politics, our children. We play cards with neighbours on Friday evenings, a tradition that started by accident and has now lasted a decade. I do admit that I sometimes go to the pub to watch big football matches. My grandchildren think our house is like a museum.

E Without social media – Lucy, 24

I deleted all my social media accounts after I realised that I was spending five hours a day scrolling. At first I worried about missing invitations, and I did miss a few. But the people who really care about me still call or send messages. I have more time and, more importantly, I no longer compare myself with everyone else's perfect lives. It was hard to explain my decision to my employer, because my job is in marketing.

Which paragraph …

  1. 0.Who originally thought the change would not last long? (A)
  2. 1.Who gave something up because of financial reasons?
  3. 2.Who has found that their family's health has improved?
  4. 3.Whose decision caused a problem at work?
  5. 4.Who now finds it difficult to find their way around?
  6. 5.Who has started a new social activity?
  7. 6.Who has become a better cook?
  8. 7.Who makes an exception for certain occasions?
  9. 8.Who no longer feels jealous of other people?
  10. 9.Who is now producing less rubbish?
naloge.rezultat:
1. A
2. A
3. E
4. B
5. D
6. C
7. D
8. E
9. C
naloge.razlaga:
Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take

  • Postopek: preberi trditve in podčrtaj ključne besede; nato preberi odstavke enega za drugim in ob vsakem preveri, katere trditve se nanj nanašajo.
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: razlaga navede del odstavka, ki pove isto kot trditev. Pozor: trditev je skoraj vedno parafraza, ne dobesedni prepis.
  • Pasti: ista beseda se pojavi v več odstavkih; pravilen je tisti, ki pove celo trditev, ne le del.

Read the text below and write the missing words in the spaces provided. There is one word missing in each gap. All contracted forms with the exception of can’t count as two words. There is an example at the beginning: Gap 0.

The science of laughter

Laughter is one of the most natural things in the world. Babies begin to laugh at around four months, long before they can speak, and people laugh in every culture on Earth. Yet scientists are still trying to understand why we do it (0) all.

Surprisingly, most laughter has very little to do with jokes. When the psychologist Robert Provine studied people laughing in everyday situations, he found that only about ten to twenty per cent of laughter followed (1) that could be described as funny. Most of the time, people laughed (2) ordinary comments such as "See you later" or "I know". This suggests that laughter is mainly a social signal: a way of showing others that we are friendly and that we belong (3) the group.

This would explain why we laugh much more when we are with other people than when we are alone. In fact, studies show that we are about thirty times more likely to laugh in company (4) on our own. Laughter is also contagious. Hearing someone else laugh activates areas in our brain (5) prepare the muscles of our face to do the same, which is why television comedies used to add recorded laughter.

Humans are not the only animals that laugh. Chimpanzees, gorillas and other apes make a breathy, panting sound when they are tickled or playing, and some scientists believe that human laughter developed (6) this. Rats, too, make high-pitched sounds when they are tickled, (7) humans cannot hear without special equipment.

Laughter also seems to be good for us. When we laugh, our bodies release chemicals called endorphins, which make us feel good and may even reduce pain. In one experiment, people who had watched a comedy were able to bear more pain than those (8) had watched a documentary. Laughing together also seems to help people bond, which may be one reason why couples who laugh together tend to stay together longer.

However, not all laughter is positive. People can laugh (9) others in order to exclude them or show that they are more powerful, and nervous laughter can be a sign of stress or embarrassment. And, of course, what one person finds funny may deeply offend another.

Some hospitals and companies now organise "laughter yoga" sessions, in which participants laugh for no reason (10) all. At first it feels strange, but because laughter is contagious, the fake laughter soon turns (11) real laughter. Whether this has the same benefits as natural laughter is still being studied.

What is clear is that laughter is far more than a reaction to a good joke. It is one of the oldest ways humans have of connecting with each other – and, as the saying goes, it may be the best medicine of (12). So the next time you feel stressed, try spending some time with friends who make you laugh. It could be good not only for your mood, but also (13) your health. After all, laughter costs nothing and has no side (14).

(Vadbeno besedilo Učilnica.com)

Read the text below and change the words in brackets so that they fit in the gaps. Write your answers in the spaces provided. There is an example at the beginning: Gap 0.

Cities that work for everybody

Imagine trying to get around your town in a wheelchair, with a baby buggy or with very poor eyesight. Suddenly, everyday obstacles such as high kerbs, broken lifts and narrow doors become serious problems. For millions of people, this is daily (0) (REAL). Inclusive design aims to change that by creating places and products that are (1) (ACCESS) to as many people as possible.

The idea is simple: instead of designing for an "average" person and then making (2) (ADAPT) for others, designers should think about the full range of human abilities from the very beginning. This approach is not only fairer, but often also more (3) (ECONOMY), because changing a building after it has been built is far more expensive than designing it (4) (CORRECT) in the first place.

Interestingly, many inventions that were originally developed for people with (5) (ABLE) are now used by everyone. Subtitles, which were introduced for deaf viewers, are now popular with people watching videos on noisy trains. Lowered kerbs help not only wheelchair users but also cyclists, parents with buggies and (6) (TRAVEL) with heavy luggage. Even the typewriter may have been invented partly to help a blind woman write letters.

Despite this progress, many cities remain (7) (FRIEND) to people with disabilities. Old buildings without lifts, public transport that is difficult to use and pavements full of parked cars and rubbish bins make it (8) (POSSIBLE) for many people to move around (9) (INDEPENDENT). In a survey in one European country, more than half of wheelchair users said that they regularly avoided going out because of such problems, which often leads to (10) (LONELY) and isolation.

Technology is helping to bring about change. Smartphone apps can now describe surroundings to blind users, and maps show which stations have working lifts. But experts warn that technology alone is not enough. Real (11) (IMPROVE) depend on political will, sufficient funding and, above all, on involving disabled people themselves in the planning process. As campaigners like to say: "Nothing about us without us."

There is also a growing (12) (AWARE) that inclusive design benefits society as a whole. As populations get older, more and more people will at some point in their lives experience (13) (DIFFICULT) with walking, seeing or hearing. A city that is designed for a child, an elderly person and a wheelchair user is a city that works better for everyone. Its streets are safer, its buildings more (14) (COMFORT) and its public spaces more (15) (WELCOME). Designing for everyone, it seems, is simply good design – and it should be the rule rather than the (16) (EXCEPT).

(Vadbeno besedilo Učilnica.com)

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to an interview with Marco Bellini, a chef who runs a restaurant that produces almost no rubbish. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Interviewer: Marco, your restaurant in Leeds doesn't have a rubbish bin. Is that true?

Marco: It's true. We have a compost bin and a recycling box for glass, but no ordinary bin. Last year, all the rubbish we couldn't recycle or compost fitted into one small bucket.

Interviewer: How is that possible in a busy restaurant?

Marco: It starts with the suppliers. We buy almost everything from local farmers, and they deliver in reusable crates, not in plastic or cardboard. Our flour comes in big cloth sacks that we send back to the mill. Milk arrives in metal churns, like fifty years ago.

Interviewer: Where did the idea come from?

Marco: From my first job, in a hotel kitchen in London. I was nineteen, and at the end of every evening I had to carry huge bags of food waste out to the bins – whole trays of bread, vegetables, even meat that nobody had touched. One night I counted: we threw away more food than we served. I couldn't sleep after that.

Interviewer: So what do you do differently?

Marco: We use every part of everything. When we cook carrots, the tops become pesto. Stale bread becomes breadcrumbs or a pudding. The bones from the meat go into stock, and vegetable peelings are dried and turned into a powder that we use for seasoning. And what really can't be eaten goes into the compost, which goes back to the farms that grow our vegetables.

Interviewer: Doesn't that limit the menu?

Marco: It makes it more creative. We don't have a fixed menu – it changes every day, depending on what the farmers bring. Customers don't choose from a long list; there are just three dishes each evening. Some people found that strange at first, but now they come precisely because they don't know what they'll get.

Interviewer: What about the customers' leftovers?

Marco: We serve smaller portions, and if people are still hungry, they can have more for free. That simple change reduced plate waste by about seventy per cent. And if someone can't finish their meal, they can take it home in a jar – but they have to bring the jar back.

Interviewer: Is it more expensive to run a restaurant like this?

Marco: At first, yes. But now we actually save money, because we buy less and waste nothing. The hardest part is the time. Making everything ourselves – butter, bread, even our own cleaning products – takes many extra hours.

Interviewer: What would you say to people who want to waste less at home?

Marco: Plan your meals and shop with a list. Freeze things before they go bad. And learn to love leftovers – yesterday's dinner can be tomorrow's lunch.

A zero-waste chef

naloge.besedilo:
You will listen to a conversation with historian Dr Clare Hughes and museum curator Sam Patel about the history of board games. You will hear the recording twice. Now read the task.

Posnetek prebere bralnik v brskalniku (angleški glas). Poslušaj ga dvakrat.
Besedilo posnetka (odpri šele po reševanju)

Presenter: With us today are historian Clare Hughes and Sam Patel, who has just opened an exhibition about board games. Clare, how old are board games?

Clare: Much older than most people think. One of the oldest we know is Senet, which was played in ancient Egypt about five thousand years ago. Boards have been found in the tombs of the pharaohs, including Tutankhamun's. The Egyptians believed the game was connected to the journey of the soul after death.

Presenter: So games weren't just for fun?

Clare: Often not. Many early games were connected with religion or used to predict the future. Others were used to teach strategy. Chess, for example, developed in India around the sixth century and was originally a kind of war game, with pieces representing infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots.

Presenter: Sam, what's the oldest object in your exhibition?

Sam: It's a set of dice made of bone, found in Turkey. They're about four thousand years old, but if you put them next to modern dice, you can hardly tell the difference. That's what I find so moving about games – people thousands of years ago enjoyed exactly the same tension when they rolled a dice.

Presenter: Are there any surprising stories in the exhibition?

Sam: Plenty. My favourite is about Monopoly. Most people think it was invented in the 1930s, but it's based on an earlier game called The Landlord's Game, designed by a woman named Elizabeth Magie in 1904. Her aim was actually to show how unfair it is when a few people own all the land. Ironically, the game became a celebration of getting rich.

Clare: There's another wonderful story from the Second World War. British intelligence produced special board game sets for prisoners of war. Hidden inside them were maps printed on silk, small compasses and real money, to help prisoners escape.

Presenter: Why do you think board games are so popular again today?

Sam: Sales have grown enormously in the last ten years. I think it's because people spend so much time looking at screens that they want to do something together, face to face. Board game cafés have opened in many cities, where you can order coffee and choose from hundreds of games.

Clare: And modern games are much more varied. In many of them, players don't compete against each other – they cooperate to beat the game itself. That's quite new.

Presenter: Sam, what do you hope visitors will take away from the exhibition?

Sam: That play isn't childish. It's one of the oldest things humans do together. And I hope they'll go home and get their old games out of the cupboard.

naloge.besedilo:
Article

Your school debate club took part in a panel discussion on inclusive education organised by a European education foundation. The editor of Education Today magazine, who moderated the discussion, has invited the clubs to write articles on the topic for the next issue. The articles should reflect the opinions of the clubs' members.

Write an article of 150–180 words with one of the following headings:
"Every child belongs in a mainstream school" or "Special schools give some children a better chance".

In your article:

  • describe the situation in your country or school,
  • present the arguments of your debate club,
  • suggest what should be done to support children with special needs.
naloge.rezultat: Članek z izbranim naslovom, pritegnitvenim uvodom, odstavki o stanju v državi ali šoli, argumentih debatnega kluba in predlogih ter z jedrnatim sklepom; 150–180 besed, polformalni slog.
naloge.razlaga:
Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Article (150–180 words), semi-formal style, with a title
  2. describe the situation in your country or school
  3. present the arguments of your debate club
  4. suggest what should be done to support children with special needs
Kako napišeš članek (article)
Članek (article): zgradba
  • Naslov: kratek in zanimiv; če navodilo ponuja naslove (headings), izberi enega in ga prepiši natančno.
  • Uvod: pritegni bralca (vprašanje, presenetljiv podatek, kratka zgodba) in v eni povedi povej, o čem bo članek.
  • Jedro: vsaka iztočnica v svojem odstavku; vsak odstavek začni s temeljno povedjo in jo podpri s primerom ali podatkom.
  • Sklep: povzemi svoje stališče ali nagovori bralce (So next time you …, why not …?). Nagovora »Dear …« in pozdrava ni.
Slog članka
  • Članek je namenjen širši javnosti (bralcem revije, šolskega časopisa, spletne strani), zato je slog polformalen: živahen, a ne pogovoren.
  • Uporabi retorična vprašanja (Have you ever wondered …?), neposreden nagovor bralca (you) in konkretne primere iz izkušenj.
  • Pri članku z mnenjem (opinion article) jasno povej svoje stališče in ga utemelji, upoštevaj tudi nasprotno mnenje.
  • Tudi v polformalnem slogu se izogibaj slengu (gonna, stuff, super cool) in pretiranim klicajem.
Uporabne zveze
  • Have you ever thought about …? · Imagine a school where … · According to a recent survey, …
  • On the one hand, … On the other hand, … · What is more, … · Not only … but also …
  • All in all, … · It is high time we … · The choice is yours.
Pogoste napake
  • Članek napisan kot pismo (Dear readers, … Yours sincerely).
  • Manjka naslov ali je naslov drugačen od ponujenega.
  • Iztočnice so le naštete, niso razvite s primeri in razlogi.
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Zgradba članka
Naslov: Every child belongs in a mainstream school
Prepiši izbrani naslov natančno.
Uvod: osebna zgodba ali vprašanje (When Tim joined our class in a wheelchair, nobody knew what to expect.).
Pritegni bralca.
Odstavek 1: stanje v naši državi / šoli
More children with special needs attend ordinary schools than ten years ago, but many buildings are not adapted.
Iztočnica 1.
Odstavek 2: argumenti debatnega kluba
Friendships, tolerance, equal opportunities; some members worried about large classes and lack of specialists.
Iztočnica 2: pokaži mnenja kluba (Most of our members believe …, A few argued …).
Odstavek 3: predlogi
Teaching assistants, smaller classes, training for teachers, accessible buildings.
Iztočnica 3: konkretni predlogi.
Sklep: Inclusion is not a favour – it is a right.
Polformalni slog, višja raven: pestro besedišče.
Preštej besede (150–180).
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
Every child belongs in a mainstream school

When Tim joined our class in a wheelchair three years ago, nobody knew what to expect. Today, he is the captain of our debate team.

In Slovenia, more children with special needs attend ordinary schools than ten years ago. However, many school buildings are still not adapted, and teachers often lack the training and support they need.

Most members of our debate club firmly believe that every child belongs in a mainstream school. Learning together builds friendships, teaches tolerance and gives all children equal opportunities. As one member put it, "Tim taught us more than any lesson about diversity." A few members, however, argued that some children need the specialist care that only special schools can provide, especially when classes are large.

So what should be done? Schools need teaching assistants, smaller classes and regular training for teachers. Every building should be fully accessible, and parents should be involved in decisions about their children's education.

Inclusion is not a favour we do for some children. It is a right that benefits us all.

Število besed: 180 (zahtevanih 150–180). Zgled je eden od mogočih odgovorov; tvoje besedilo je lahko drugačno, a mora izpolniti vse zahteve iz navodila.

George Orwell: Animal Farm

Write an essay of 250–300 words. Do not write about the text and/or the author in general.
naloge.rezultat: Esej s tezo o Napoleonu, ki oblast pridobi in ohrani s silo, propagando in strahom, podprto s prizori (psi in izgon Snowballa, Squealer, kult osebnosti, usmrtitve, ukinitev sestankov, spreminjanje zapovedi, sklepni prizor); brez obnove; 250–300 besed.

Kaj zahteva navodilo: kontrolni seznam

Vsaka vrstica je ena zahteva. Vsaka mora biti v tvojem besedilu jasno vidna (najbolje v svojem odstavku); ko jo napišeš, jo odkljukaj.

  1. Discuss how Napoleon gains and keeps power in George Orwell's Animal Farm.
  2. Do not write about the text and/or the author in general (no plot summary, no biography).
  3. Write 250–300 words.
Kako napišeš esej o književnem delu
Esej o književnem delu: zgradba
  • Uvod: avtor, naslov in teza, ki neposredno odgovori na navodilo (Will Freeman changes from a selfish man into …). Brez življenjepisa avtorja.
  • Jedro: dva do trije odstavki, vsak z eno trditvijo. Vsako trditev podpri s konkretnim prizorom ali kratkim navedkom in razloži, kaj pokaže (to je analiza).
  • Primerjava (če gre za dve deli): primerjaj neposredno z »Whereas …«, »Similarly, …«, »In contrast, …«, ne napiši dveh ločenih esejev.
  • Sklep: vrni se k tezi in pokaži, kaj pove o delu kot celoti.
Analiza namesto obnove
  • Navodilo pravi »Do not write about the text and/or the author in general«: ne obnavljaj zgodbe in ne piši splošno o avtorju.
  • Zgradba odstavka PEA: Point (trditev) → Evidence (prizor, navedek) → Analysis (kaj to pomeni za temo).
  • Uporabljaj sedanjik za dogajanje v delu (Will lies to the single mothers …).
  • Glagoli za analizo: shows, suggests, reveals, highlights, emphasises, symbolises.
Uporabne zveze
  • This is evident when … · A turning point comes when … · This scene suggests that …
  • At the beginning of the novel, … By the end, … · Gradually, …
  • Whereas X …, Y … · Both novels show … · Unlike …, …
Ocenjevanje in postopek pisanja
Kako ocenjujejo pisni sestavek
  • Vsebina: ali si odgovoril na vse iztočnice (alineje) iz navodila in ali je vsaka dovolj razvita (ne le omenjena v pol povedi). Manjkajoča iztočnica je največja izguba točk.
  • Zgradba in oblika: odstavki, logično zaporedje, povezovalci (linking words), oblika, ki ustreza besedilni vrsti (nagovor in pozdrav pri e-pismu, glava in podnaslovi pri poročilu).
  • Besedišče: pestro, natančno in primerno slogu; isto besedo ne ponavljaj, uporabi sopomenke.
  • Slovnica in pravopis: pravilni časi, ujemanje osebka in glagola (he goes), členi (a/an/the), predlogi, velika začetnica in ločila.
  • Dolžina: drži se razpona besed iz navodila. Prekratko besedilo navadno ne pokrije vseh iztočnic, predolgo pa izgubi točke za obliko.
Postopek v petih korakih
  • 1. Preberi navodilo dvakrat in podčrtaj: komu pišeš, zakaj pišeš (pritožba, prijava, poročilo …) in vse iztočnice.
  • 2. Naredi načrt: ob vsako iztočnico napiši dve do tri ključne besede in konkreten podatek (številko, datum, primer).
  • 3. Piši po odstavkih: praviloma ena iztočnica = en odstavek. Vsak odstavek začni s povedjo, ki pove, o čem govori.
  • 4. Preveri slog: formalno besedilo nima skrajšanih oblik (I'm → I am), pogovornih izrazov (stuff, a lot of → a great deal of) in klicajev.
  • 5. Preštej besede in popravi: preveri čase, -s v 3. osebi ednine, člene in črkovanje.
Načrt po korakih
Načrt eseja
Uvod: teza – Napoleon gains and keeps power through force, propaganda and fear, turning the revolution into a dictatorship.
Teza v uvodu, brez obnove.
Jedro 1 – force: he secretly raises Jessie's and Bluebell's puppies; the dogs chase Snowball off the farm.
Ključni prizor prevzema oblasti.
Jedro 2 – propaganda: Squealer explains every decision; Snowball is blamed for everything; the song 'Comrade Napoleon' and his many titles.
Kult osebnosti.
Jedro 3 – fear and privilege: the show trials and executions; the meetings are abolished; the pigs move into the farmhouse and change the commandments.
Teror in privilegiji.
Sklep: at the end the pigs cannot be told apart from humans – Napoleon has become the tyrant the animals rebelled against.
Sklep se vrne k tezi.
Merila: vsebina in interpretacija, zgradba, jezik. 250–300 besed.
Zgledno besedilo (eden od mogočih odgovorov)
How Napoleon gains and keeps power in Animal Farm

In George Orwell's Animal Farm, the animals rebel against Mr Jones in order to create a society in which all animals are equal. Yet within a few years, the pig Napoleon has become a tyrant far crueller than Jones. He gains and keeps his power through a combination of force, propaganda and fear.

Napoleon prepares his rise to power long before he uses it. He takes the puppies of Jessie and Bluebell, saying he will educate them, and secretly raises them as his private guard. When Snowball presents his plans for the windmill, Napoleon gives a high-pitched whimper, and nine huge dogs chase his rival off the farm. From that moment, nobody dares to oppose him openly.

However, force alone is not enough. Napoleon relies on Squealer to explain every decision and to convince the animals that he is acting for their benefit. Snowball is blamed for every problem, from the collapse of the windmill to broken windows. At the same time, a cult of personality develops: Napoleon receives titles such as "Father of All Animals", and a poem praising him is painted on the barn wall.

Finally, Napoleon rules through fear and privilege. Sunday meetings are abolished, and animals who confess to imaginary crimes are executed in front of everyone. Meanwhile, the pigs move into the farmhouse, sleep in beds and drink alcohol, changing the commandments to justify their behaviour.

In conclusion, Napoleon's rise shows how a revolution can be betrayed by those who lead it. In the final scene, the animals look from pig to man and cannot tell the difference. Orwell warns that power without control inevitably corrupts.

The Library That Wouldn't Close

When the town council of Ashford announced in January that its small public library would close at the end of the school year, most people were sad but not surprised. The building was old, the heating often failed, and the number of visitors had been falling for years. Only one person refused to accept the decision: eleven-year-old Ruby Shaw.

Ruby had been visiting the library twice a week since she was four. "My mum works late, so the library was where I waited for her after school," she explains. "The librarian, Mrs Okafor, helped me with my homework and always kept the newest books for me. It was like a second home."

Ruby started by writing a letter to the local newspaper. In it, she explained that many children in the town did not have books at home or a quiet place to study. The newspaper printed the letter on its front page, and within a week Ruby had received more than three hundred replies from people who agreed with her.

Encouraged by this, Ruby set up an online petition. Her older brother helped her make a short video, in which she walked around the library and talked about what it meant to her. The video was shared thousands of times, and a famous children's author who had grown up in the town posted it on her own website. By March, the petition had over twelve thousand signatures – more than the population of the town.

The council agreed to listen. Ruby was invited to speak at a council meeting, the youngest person ever to do so. She was so nervous that her hands were shaking, but she spoke for five minutes without notes. "Libraries are not just about books," she told the councillors. "They are about giving everyone the same chance."

In the end, the council found a compromise. The library would stay open, but it would move into a room in the town's community centre, which was cheaper to heat. Volunteers offered to help Mrs Okafor run it, and local businesses donated money for new computers and furniture.

The new library opened in September. On the first day, more than four hundred people came, and Ruby was asked to cut the ribbon. She now runs a reading club for younger children every Saturday morning. "I didn't think I could change anything," she says. "But if you care about something enough, people will listen."

Spodaj je pri vsaki postavki rešitev in razlaga, ki pokaže, kje v besedilu ali posnetku je odgovor in katero pravilo velja.

1. B
»told that« + stavek: I would be responsible for them day and night.
2. C
»terrified that« + stavek: I would lose one of them in the forest.
3. D
»by the time the children were asleep,« – glavni stavek: I was usually too tired even to read.
4. E
»Some of them« + povedek: had never spent a night away; sledi jok zaradi domotožja.
5. F
»He refused to take part in anything and« – vzporedni povedek: spent most of his time sitting alone.
6. G
»to my surprise« + kratek glavni stavek: he said yes.
7. H
»his face was shining, and« – nadaljevanje: he asked whether he could do it again.
8. I
»I learned that I am more patient than I thought, and« + that-stavek: that I actually enjoy being responsible.
9. J
»stay calm when« + stavek: something goes wrong; sledi primer (»such as when …«).
10. K
»primary education at university,« – pristavek: something I would never have considered before; sledi »If someone had told me that a year ago …«.

naloge.besedilo:
Read the text below and write the missing words in the spaces provided. There is one word missing in each gap. All contracted forms with the exception of can’t count as two words. There is an example at the beginning: Gap 0.

The world's first underground railway

On 10 January 1863, thousands of Londoners queued to travel (0) something completely new: a railway under the ground. The Metropolitan Railway ran for about six kilometres between Paddington and Farringdon, and (1) the first day alone it carried almost forty thousand passengers.

The railway was built to solve a serious problem. In the middle of the nineteenth century, London's streets were so crowded with horses, carts and people (2) it could take hours to cross the city. Building roads was impossible, so engineers decided to go underground instead. Most of the first line was built using the "cut and cover" method: workers dug a deep trench along a street, built the tunnel inside it and then covered it (3) again.

The early trains were pulled by steam engines, (4) filled the tunnels with smoke. Passengers often arrived at their destination covered in dirt, and some complained that they could hardly breathe. The situation improved only in 1890, (5) the first deep electric line opened. Its tunnels were round, like tubes, which is why Londoners still call the Underground "the Tube".

During the Second World War, the Underground played an unexpected role. When German planes bombed London, thousands of people spent their nights sleeping (6) the platforms, which were among the safest places in the city. Some stations even had libraries, first-aid posts and entertainment.

One of the Underground's most famous features is its map. Before 1933, maps showed the lines exactly (7) they ran under the streets, which made them confusing. An engineer called Harry Beck had the idea of drawing a simple diagram, (8) straight lines and stations at equal distances, like an electrical circuit. At first, the managers thought nobody would understand it, but passengers loved it, and the design has been copied (9) cities all over the world.

Today, the Underground has around 270 stations and carries several million passengers a day. It has also given the English language a famous phrase: "Mind the gap", the warning to be careful of the space between the train (10) the platform.

However, the oldest underground railway in the world also faces problems. Many trains and tunnels are old, and in summer the temperature on some lines can become extremely high, because the deep tunnels have no air conditioning. New lines are being built, but such projects are hugely expensive and take many years (11) complete.

More than a century and a half after its opening, the Underground is still the heart of London. For millions of people, it is simply the fastest way to get from A to B. But it is (12) a piece of living history – and for many tourists, a ride on the Tube is just (13) important as a visit to Big Ben.

(Vadbeno besedilo Učilnica.com)

Example: 0. on / in
naloge.rezultat:
1. on
2. that
3. up / over
4. which
5. when
6. on
7. as / where
8. with
9. in / by
10. and
11. to
12. also
13. as
naloge.razlaga:
Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take
  • Kaj zahteva naloga: v vsako vrzel napisati eno besedo. Navadno manjkajo slovnične besede: členi (a, the), predlogi (in, on, at), vezniki (although, because), oziralni zaimki (who, which, that), pomožni glagoli (have, is, did), primerjave (as, than).
  • Postopek: preberi celo poved; ugotovi, katera besedna vrsta manjka. Nato preveri ustaljene zveze (depend on, used to, as … as).
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: razlaga pove slovnično pravilo ali ustaljeno zvezo, ki zahteva prav to besedo. Kjer je več pravilnih rešitev, so navedene vse (ločene s poševnico).
  • Pasti: dve besedi v eni vrzeli; beseda, ki se pomensko ujema, a slovnično ne (who za stvari, that za vejico).

Spodaj je pri vsaki postavki rešitev in razlaga, ki pokaže, kje v besedilu ali posnetku je odgovor in katero pravilo velja.

1. on
»on the first day« = na prvi dan.
2. that
»so crowded … that« = tako natrpane, da.
3. up / over
»cover it up / over« = prekriti.
4. which
Oziralni zaimek za stvari (steam engines) za vejico.
5. when
Časovni veznik po letnici: in 1890, when …
6. on
»on the platforms« = na peronih.
7. as / where
»exactly as / where they ran« = natanko tako, kot / kjer so potekale.
8. with
»a diagram with straight lines« = z ravnimi črtami.
9. in / by
»copied in cities all over the world« ali »by cities«.
10. and
»between A and B«.
11. to
»take many years to complete« = traja mnogo let.
12. also
»But it is also …« = je pa tudi.
13. as
»just as important as« = enako pomembno kot.

naloge.besedilo:
Read the text below and write the correct form of the verbs in brackets in the spaces provided. There is an example at the beginning: Gap 0.

Wonderful things

For years, the British archaeologist Howard Carter (0) (SEARCH) the Valley of the Kings in Egypt for the tomb of a little-known pharaoh called Tutankhamun. By 1922, his sponsor, Lord Carnarvon, (1) (SPEND) a fortune on the excavations and was ready to give up. He agreed to pay for just one more season.

On 4 November 1922, a boy who (2) (BRING) water to the workers found a stone step in the sand. Carter's team soon uncovered a staircase that led down to a sealed door. Carter immediately (3) (SEND) a telegram to Carnarvon, who travelled from England to be present when the tomb (4) (OPEN).

On 26 November, Carter made a small hole in the door and held up a candle. As his eyes (5) (ADJUST) to the darkness, he saw gold glittering everywhere. When Carnarvon asked whether he could see anything, Carter famously replied: "Yes, wonderful things."

The tomb was the most complete royal burial that (6) (EVER / DISCOVER) in Egypt. Unlike most other tombs, it (7) (NOT / ROB) completely in ancient times, and it contained more than five thousand objects, including furniture, chariots, jewellery and the famous golden mask that (8) (COVER) the face of the young king's mummy.

Just a few months after the discovery, Lord Carnarvon (9) (DIE) of an infected mosquito bite. Newspapers soon began to write about a "curse of the pharaohs", which supposedly punished anyone who disturbed the tomb. In reality, most of the people who (10) (WORK) in the tomb lived for many years, including Carter himself.

It took Carter and his team about ten years to record and remove all the objects. Today, many of them (11) (DISPLAY) in museums in Cairo, and they attract millions of visitors. Scientists still (12) (STUDY) the mummy of Tutankhamun to find out how the king, who was only about nineteen when he died, really lost his life. If Carnarvon (13) (REFUSE) to pay for that last season, the tomb might still be buried under the sand.

Example: 0. had searched / had been searching
naloge.rezultat:
1. had spent
2. was bringing / brought
3. sent
4. was opened
5. adjusted / were adjusting
6. had ever been discovered
7. had not been robbed
8. covered / had covered
9. died
10. worked / had worked
11. are displayed
12. are studying / study
13. had refused
naloge.razlaga:
Kako rešiš to nalogo in zakaj so rešitve take
  • Kaj zahteva naloga: glagol v oklepaju napisati v pravilni obliki (čas, trpnik, nedoločnik, -ing, pogojnik).
  • Postopek: poišči časovne izraze (yesterday, since, for, by the time, next week) in osebek (ednina ali množina, ali osebek dejanje opravlja ali ga trpi). Preveri tudi besede pred vrzeljo, ki zahtevajo določeno obliko (enjoy + -ing, decide + to, would rather + nedoločnik).
  • Zakaj je odgovor pravilen: razlaga pove, kateri časovni izraz ali zgradba zahteva to obliko.
  • Pasti: pozabljen -s v 3. osebi ednine, napačen pomožni glagol v trpniku, past simple namesto present perfect ob since/for.

Spodaj je pri vsaki postavki rešitev in razlaga, ki pokaže, kje v besedilu ali posnetku je odgovor in katero pravilo velja.

1. had spent
»By 1922« – dejanje pred trenutkom v preteklosti: past perfect.
2. was bringing / brought
Dejanje v teku v ozadju (past continuous) ali navada (brought).
3. sent
Nepravilni glagol send – sent – sent.
4. was opened
Trpnik v pretekliku: when the tomb was opened.
5. adjusted / were adjusting
»As his eyes adjusted« – postopno dogajanje v preteklosti.
6. had ever been discovered
Presežnik + »ever« v preteklosti: past perfect passive.
7. had not been robbed
Pred odkritjem, trpnik: past perfect passive.
8. covered / had covered
Stanje v preteklosti: the mask that covered the face.
9. died
Zaključeno dejanje: past simple.
10. worked / had worked
Dejanje v preteklosti (past simple ali past perfect).
11. are displayed
Danes, trpnik: present simple passive.
12. are studying / study
»still« – trenutno, dalj časa trajajoče dejanje: present continuous ali simple.
13. had refused
Tretji pogojnik: If Carnarvon had refused …, the tomb might still be buried.
